93777.m: In molten salt electrolysis, a melt is split up.

93778.q: Which metal is obtained by electrolysis of molten table salt?
93778.e: Table salt is sodium chloride. In the electrolysis of the melt, sodium forms at the negative pole and chlorine at the positive pole.
93778.m: Sodium is obtained from molten table salt.

93779.q: In which canton is Chippis, with its well-known aluminium works?
93779.e: Chippis lies near Sierre in the Rhône valley. The aluminium works have shaped the village for over a hundred years.
93779.m: The Chippis aluminium works are in Valais.

93780.q: From which raw material is aluminium obtained?
93780.e: Bauxite is a reddish rock with a lot of aluminium oxide. Aluminium is made from it in several steps.

93781.q: Why was an aluminium works built in a mountain valley in Valais, as at Chippis?
a: Because of water power for lots of electricity
Because of the many bauxite mines there
93781.e: Aluminium electrolysis needs an enormous amount of electricity. The mountain streams of Valais supplied it cheaply from water power.
93781.m: Water power made Valais attractive for aluminium works.

93782.q: Why is aluminium popular for vehicles and aircraft?
a: It is light and hardly corrodes
93782.e: Aluminium has a much lower density than steel. It also protects itself from corrosion with a thin oxide layer.
93782.m: Aluminium is light and hardly corrodes.

93783.q: Which process uses electric current to obtain aluminium?
93783.e: In electrolysis, electric current separates the aluminium from its compound. This needs a lot of electricity.

93784.q: Which things made of aluminium does almost every child know?
93784.e: Aluminium can easily be rolled into thin sheets and foils. Drinks cans and kitchen foil, for example, are made from it.
93784.m: Cans and kitchen foil are made of aluminium.

93785.q: Why is it especially worthwhile to recycle aluminium?
a: It needs much less energy than making it new
New aluminium can no longer be made
93785.e: Making it from bauxite needs an enormous amount of electricity. Melting down old aluminium saves most of this energy.
93785.m: Recycling aluminium saves a lot of energy.

93786.q: On which large river does Chippis lie?
93786.e: Chippis lies on the left bank of the Rhône. The Navisence from the Val d’Anniviers also flows into it there.

93787.q: What do you do when electroplating?
a: Coat an object with metal using electricity
93787.e: In electroplating, metal ions move from a solution onto the workpiece. There they form a thin layer of metal.

93788.q: In electroplating, which pole is the object to be coated connected to?
93788.e: The metal ions in the solution are positively charged. They are attracted by the negative pole and settle there as metal.
93788.m: In electroplating, the workpiece hangs on the negative pole.

93789.q: What do you absolutely need for electroplating?
93789.e: Only the current makes the metal ions move to the workpiece. There they settle as a thin layer of metal.
93789.m: Electroplating only works with electric current.

93790.q: What is electroplating with chromium called, for example on shiny taps?
93790.e: A layer of chromium is hard, shiny and resists corrosion. That is why many taps and fittings are chrome-plated.

93791.q: What must be dissolved in the liquid of an electroplating bath for a layer of silver to form?
93791.e: The solution contains a silver salt. The positively charged silver ions become silver metal on the workpiece.
93791.m: For a silver layer, the bath needs silver ions.

93792.q: In electroplating, what often happens to an anode made of the coating metal?
93792.e: At the positive pole, metal atoms go into solution as ions. This supplies the metal that settles on the workpiece.
93792.m: In electroplating, the metal anode supplies new ions.

93793.q: Why is cheap jewellery often gold-plated instead of made of pure gold?
a: A thin layer of gold is much cheaper
Gold is too light for jewellery
93793.e: In gold plating, only a wafer-thin layer of gold is applied. It looks like gold but uses very little of it.

93794.q: Apart from making things look nicer, what is electroplating often used for?
93794.e: A layer of metal can protect the base material from rust. Many screws, for example, are zinc-plated.
93794.m: Electroplated layers often protect against corrosion.

93795.q: Which energy conversion takes place in a battery when it powers a device?
93795.e: Chemical reactions take place in the battery in which electrons flow. This produces electric current.
93795.m: A battery turns chemical energy into electrical energy.

93796.q: Which Italian scientist built the first battery around 1800?
93796.e: Volta stacked zinc and copper discs with soaked cardboard in between. This voltaic pile was the first to supply a steady current.
93796.m: Alessandro Volta built the first battery around 1800.

93797.q: What voltage does an ordinary AA alkaline battery have?
93797.e: An alkaline manganese cell supplies 1.5 volts. For 9 volts, several cells are connected together in one block.

93798.q: Which rechargeable batteries are in most mobile phones and electric cars today?
93798.e: Lithium-ion batteries store a lot of energy for little weight. That is why they are used in mobile phones, laptops and electric cars.
93798.m: Mobile phones mostly run on lithium-ion batteries.

93799.q: What rule applies in Switzerland to shops that sell batteries?
a: They must take back used batteries free of charge
They may only sell rechargeable batteries
They must not take back batteries
93799.e: In Switzerland, shops are obliged to take batteries back. Disposal is paid for by an advance fee when you buy them.
93799.m: You take used batteries back to the shop.

93800.q: Why don’t old batteries belong in the household rubbish?
a: They contain pollutants and valuable metals
They are too heavy for the rubbish bag
They dissolve in the rubbish at once
They charge up again in the rubbish
93800.e: Batteries can contain poisonous substances that harm the environment. Also, metals such as zinc, nickel or lithium can be recovered.
93800.m: Batteries belong at the collection point.

93801.q: What is the battery pole called from which electrons flow into the circuit when it discharges?
93801.e: At the negative pole, electrons are released by the chemical reaction. They flow through the device to the positive pole.
93801.m: Electrons flow from the negative to the positive pole.

93802.q: Which two metals are often pushed into a lemon to build a lemon battery?
93802.e: You need two different metals as electrodes. Copper and zinc work well because they differ in how reactive they are.
93802.m: For a lemon battery you need copper and zinc.

93803.q: What does the lemon juice do in a lemon battery?
a: It conducts the ions as an electrolyte
It supplies all the energy as sugar
It insulates the metals from each other
93803.e: The sour juice contains dissolved ions and so completes the circuit inside the battery. Without an electrolyte, no current flows.
93803.m: The lemon juice acts as the electrolyte in the battery.

93804.q: Why does a light bulb usually not light up with a single lemon battery?
a: The voltage and current are too small
Lemon juice does not conduct electricity at all
93804.e: A lemon supplies just under 1 volt and only a very small current. That is not enough for a light bulb.
93804.m: A single lemon supplies too little current for a light bulb.

93805.q: How do you increase the voltage when you use several lemon batteries?
a: You put them in the fridge
93805.e: In a series circuit, the copper of one lemon is connected to the zinc of the next. The voltages add up.
93805.m: Lemons connected in series give more voltage.

93806.q: Which metal is the negative pole in a lemon battery?
93806.e: Zinc is more reactive than copper and gives up electrons more easily. It slowly dissolves and forms the negative pole.
93806.m: In a lemon battery, zinc is the negative pole.

93807.q: How many lemons of about 0.9 volts each do you need at least in series for 2.5 volts?
93807.e: Two lemons give 2 times 0.9 volts, so 1.8 volts, which is too little. Three lemons give 3 times 0.9 volts, so 2.7 volts.
93807.m: Three lemons in series supply about 2.7 volts.

93808.q: What can you use to check whether a lemon battery is supplying voltage?
93808.e: A voltmeter measures the electrical voltage between the two metals. You connect it to the copper and the zinc.
93808.m: A voltmeter measures the voltage of the lemon battery.

93809.q: With which other fruit or vegetable does this kind of battery also work?
93809.e: Potatoes and apples also contain water with dissolved ions. So they can serve as an electrolyte too.
93809.m: You can also build a battery with a potato.

93810.q: What makes a metal a precious metal?
a: It hardly reacts with air and water
It is as light as polystyrene
93810.e: Precious metals such as gold and platinum resist corrosion very well. They do not rust and keep their shine.
93810.m: Precious metals hardly react with air and water.

93811.q: Which of these metals is a precious metal?
93811.e: Platinum, like gold and silver, is a precious metal. Iron, aluminium and zinc are base metals.

93812.q: What is the chemical symbol for silver?
93812.e: The symbol Ag comes from the Latin word “argentum” for silver. Si stands for silicon.

93813.q: How much pure gold does 18-carat gold contain?
93813.e: Pure gold is 24 carat. 18 divided by 24 gives 0.75, so 75 per cent gold.
93813.m: 18 carat means three quarters pure gold.

93814.q: What role does Switzerland play in the world gold trade?
a: A large share of the gold is refined here
It has the biggest gold mines
Gold is made from lead here
93814.e: Several large gold refineries, mainly in Ticino, purify gold from all over the world. That makes Switzerland a centre of the gold trade.
93814.m: A lot of gold is refined in Switzerland.

93815.q: In which part of a car are precious metals such as palladium and rhodium used?
93815.e: In the catalytic converter, palladium and rhodium help turn poisonous exhaust gases into less harmful substances. They are not used up themselves.

93816.q: Which mixture of two acids can even dissolve gold?
93816.e: Aqua regia, or “royal water”, is a mixture of hydrochloric acid and nitric acid. It dissolves gold, which otherwise can hardly be attacked.

93817.q: Why does silver cutlery go dark over time?
a: It reacts with sulfur compounds in the air
It takes on colour from food
93817.e: Silver forms a dark layer of silver sulfide with sulfur compounds. This can be polished off again.
93817.m: Silver tarnishes because of sulfur compounds.

93818.q: Which two substances does iron need in order to rust?
93818.e: Iron only rusts when moisture and oxygen are both present. In dry air it hardly rusts.
93818.m: Iron rusts with water and oxygen.

93819.q: What is the greenish layer called that forms on copper roofs over time and protects the copper?
93819.e: Copper slowly reacts with substances in the air. This produces a green patina that protects the metal beneath.
93819.m: The green patina protects copper roofs.

93820.q: What is a sacrificial anode on a ship’s hull?
a: A piece of more reactive metal that corrodes instead of the hull
93820.e: A more reactive metal such as zinc or magnesium is connected to the steel hull. It dissolves first and so protects the steel.
93820.m: A sacrificial anode corrodes instead of the steel.

93821.q: What is a simple way to protect bare tools from rust?
a: With a thin film of oil
93821.e: A film of oil stops water and oxygen reaching the iron. That is why tools and bicycle chains are oiled.
93821.m: A film of oil protects iron from rust.

93822.q: Why doesn’t aluminium rust right through, even though it is a base metal?
a: A thin oxide layer protects it
Aluminium is always covered with paint
93822.e: In air, a thin, dense oxide layer forms on aluminium straight away. It protects the metal beneath from further corrosion.
93822.m: A thin oxide layer protects aluminium.

93823.q: Which simple method protects an iron garden gate from rust?
93823.e: The paint forms a layer that keeps water and oxygen away from the iron. If it is damaged, rust can form there.
93823.m: Anti-rust paint keeps water and oxygen away from iron.

93824.q: Why is rust on iron so harmful, while the layer on aluminium protects it?
a: Rust is loose and flakes off
93824.e: Rust is porous and lets water and air keep reaching the iron. So the corrosion eats deeper and deeper.
93824.m: Loose rust does not protect the iron.

a: The destruction of a metal by chemical reaction with its surroundings
The melting of a metal in a furnace
93825.e: Corrosion is a chemical reaction of the metal with substances from its surroundings, such as oxygen and water. Rusting is the corrosion of iron.
93825.m: Corrosion is chemical attack on metals.

a: Steel parts are dipped in liquid zinc
93826.e: The steel parts are dipped in a bath of molten zinc. Afterwards they are covered with a firm layer of zinc.
93826.m: In hot-dip galvanising, steel is dipped in liquid zinc.

93827.q: Roughly how hot is a zinc bath in hot-dip galvanising?
93827.e: Zinc melts at around 420 degrees. So the bath is kept at about 450 degrees.
93827.m: A zinc bath is around 450 degrees hot.

93828.q: Why does a zinc layer still protect the steel even when it is scratched?
a: Zinc is more reactive and corrodes first
93828.e: Zinc gives up electrons more easily than iron. So at a scratch the zinc corrodes first, and the steel next to it stays protected.
93828.m: Zinc protects steel even at scratches.

93829.q: Which parts along Swiss roads are typically hot-dip galvanised?
93829.e: Crash barriers stand outdoors all year and get splashed with salt water in winter. The zinc layer reliably protects them from rust.

93830.q: What is done to steel parts before hot-dip galvanising so that the zinc sticks well?
93830.e: In pickling, acid removes rust and scale from the surface. Zinc only bonds well to clean steel.
93830.m: Before galvanising, the steel is pickled.

93831.q: What forms at the boundary between steel and zinc in hot-dip galvanising?
93831.e: In the hot bath, iron and zinc combine at the surface. This makes the layer stick very firmly to the steel.
93831.m: Hot-dip galvanising forms an iron-zinc alloy.

93832.q: What does freshly hot-dip galvanised steel often look like?
a: Shiny silver with a crystal pattern
93832.e: The zinc layer shines silver and often shows a pattern of zinc crystals. Over time it turns dull grey.

93833.q: Which large pharmaceutical company has its headquarters in Basel?
93833.e: Novartis is one of the largest pharmaceutical companies in the world and is based in Basel. Nestlé is based in Vevey, Swatch in Biel and Swisscom in Bern.
93833.m: Novartis has its headquarters in Basel.

93834.q: What happened on 1 November 1986 at Schweizerhalle near Basel?
a: A chemical warehouse burnt down and poisoned the Rhine
A nuclear power station was opened
A new bridge over the Rhine collapsed
93834.e: When a Sandoz warehouse caught fire, firefighting water carrying chemicals flowed into the river. Fish and other animals died along many kilometres.
93834.m: The Schweizerhalle fire in 1986 caused a huge fish kill.

93835.q: What do the Basel companies Roche and Novartis mainly make?
93835.e: Roche and Novartis are among the largest pharmaceutical companies in the world. They develop and sell medicines.
93835.m: Basel is a centre of the pharmaceutical industry.

93836.q: Which river was important to Basel’s chemical industry as a transport route and water source?
93836.e: Raw materials could be delivered by ship along the Rhine. The factories also needed a lot of water.
93836.m: The Rhine was central to Basel’s chemical industry.

93837.q: What was DDT, discovered in Basel, used for?
93837.e: In 1939 it was discovered in Basel that DDT kills insects. Later it was banned in many countries because of the harm it does to the environment.

93838.q: What does the Basel company Syngenta mainly make?
93838.e: Syngenta is an agrochemical company. It sells products against pests and seeds for farming.

93839.q: Which building in Basel, at 205 metres, is the tallest in Switzerland (as of 2025)?
93839.e: The Roche Tower Building 2 was completed in 2022 and is 205 metres tall. It towers over the neighbouring Building 1, which is 178 metres.
93839.m: Switzerland’s tallest tower belongs to Roche in Basel.

93840.q: How long does hot-dip galvanising typically protect steel outdoors?
93840.e: The zinc layer wears away only very slowly. Depending on the surroundings, the protection often lasts from 25 to over 50 years.
93840.m: Hot-dip galvanising protects steel for decades.

93841.q: What does the figure 999.9 on a gold bar mean?
a: It is 999.9 parts per thousand gold
It was made in the year 999
93841.e: The number gives the purity in thousandths. 999.9 means almost pure gold.
93841.m: A bar marked 999.9 is almost pure gold.

93842.q: What did many Basel chemical companies start out making in the 19th century?
93842.e: Basel’s silk ribbon industry needed a lot of colours. So the first chemical companies made artificial dyes.
93842.m: Basel’s chemical industry began with dyes.

93843.q: What is slag from the blast furnace often used for afterwards?
a: As a building material, for example for cement
93843.e: Cooled blast furnace slag is a stone-like material. It is used in road building and to make cement.
93843.m: Blast furnace slag is used as a building material.

93844.q: Why must a workpiece be thoroughly cleaned and degreased before electroplating?
a: So that the metal layer sticks well
93844.e: Grease and dirt stop the metal settling directly on the surface. Otherwise the layer flakes off later.
93844.m: An electroplated layer only sticks to clean surfaces.

93845.q: In what form is data sent through a fibre optic cable?
93845.e: In an optical fibre, data is sent as very fast pulses of light. A light signal can stand for a 1, for example, and no light for a 0.
93845.m: Fibre optic cables send data with light.

93846.q: Which physical effect traps the light inside an optical fibre?
93846.e: If the light hits the boundary between two layers of glass at a shallow enough angle, it is completely reflected back. This guides the light even round bends.
93846.m: Total internal reflection keeps the light trapped in the optical fibre.

93847.q: What is the innermost part of an optical fibre called, where the light travels?
93847.e: An optical fibre consists of a thin core and a cladding around it. The core has a higher refractive index than the cladding, so the light stays in the core.
93847.m: The light travels in the core of the fibre, and the cladding surrounds it.

93848.q: What raw material is the glass for optical fibres mainly made from?
93848.e: Optical fibres for data lines are made of very pure quartz glass, that is silicon dioxide. This glass is so clear that light can travel many kilometres.
93848.m: Optical fibres are made of very pure quartz glass.

93849.q: What advantage does a fibre optic cable have over a copper cable?
a: It is not affected by electrical interference
93849.e: Light in glass is not disturbed by electric and magnetic fields. In addition, an optical fibre can carry much more data over longer distances.
93849.m: Fibre optics are fast and unaffected by electrical interference.

93850.q: Why is the internet faster when the optical fibre goes all the way into the flat?
a: The data doesn't have to travel over old copper lines
The flat is then closer to the satellite
93850.e: Optical fibre can carry much more data than a copper cable. If it goes all the way into the flat, there is no slow copper section left.
93850.m: Fibre right into the flat makes the internet fast.

93851.q: How do fibre optic cables mainly connect the continents for the internet?
a: As undersea cables on the seabed
93851.e: By far the largest part of international data traffic runs through undersea cables with optical fibres on the seabed. Satellites only carry a small part.
93851.m: Undersea fibre optic cables connect the continents.

93852.q: Roughly how thin is a single optical fibre?
a: About as thin as a hair
About as thick as a pencil
About as thick as a garden hose
About as thick as an arm
93852.e: An optical fibre is about a tenth of a millimetre thick. A cable often contains many such fibres in a protective sheath.
93852.m: An optical fibre is as thin as a hair.

93853.q: What kind of light is mostly used in fibre optic networks?
93853.e: Data networks mostly use infrared light with wavelengths of around 1300 or 1550 nanometres. In these ranges the light is weakened especially little in the glass.
93853.m: Fibre optic networks mostly use invisible infrared light.

93854.q: What does roaming mean for mobile phones?
a: The phone uses another network abroad
The phone switches to flight mode
93854.e: Abroad your own provider's network is usually not available. When roaming, the phone logs into a partner network, which often costs extra.
93854.m: When roaming, the phone uses a partner network abroad.

93855.q: Which emergency number works all over Europe, including from a mobile phone?
93855.e: 112 is the standard European emergency number and works in all EU countries and in Switzerland. In Switzerland there are also 117 (police), 118 (fire brigade) and 144 (ambulance).
93855.m: The emergency number 112 works all over Europe.

93856.q: What happens during a so-called handover while you are on the phone in a moving train?
a: The call is passed on to the next radio cell
The phone switches to a landline
93856.e: When you move, the network passes the connection from one radio cell to the next. Ideally, the call does not drop.
93856.m: During a handover the connection moves from cell to cell.

93857.q: What does the abbreviation SIM stand for in SIM card?
93857.e: The SIM card is the “Subscriber Identity Module”. It identifies the phone on the network as a customer of a particular provider.
93857.m: The SIM card identifies you on the mobile network.

93858.q: With which 2nd-generation mobile standard was the text message (SMS) introduced?
93858.e: GSM is the standard of the second mobile generation (2G). It brought digital calls and the short text message, SMS.
93858.m: Text messages came with the digital GSM network.

93859.q: What did the first text message, sent in 1992, say?
93859.e: On 3 December 1992 the engineer Neil Papworth sent the message “Merry Christmas” from a computer to a mobile phone. This is considered the first text message.
93859.m: The first text message wished people a merry Christmas in 1992.

93860.e: LTE stands for “Long Term Evolution” and is the fourth mobile generation. Above all it brought much faster mobile internet.

93861.q: What is the aerial site called through which mobile phones are connected to the mobile network?
93861.e: A base station consists of aerials and equipment that talk by radio to the phones in its cell. From there the data usually travels on by cable.
93861.m: Mobile phones send signals to the nearest base station.

93863.q: What does the “G” in the name 5G stand for?
93863.e: 5G is the fifth generation of mobile communications. Each new generation has so far mainly brought faster data transmission.

93864.q: What does very low latency, which 5G is supposed to make possible, mean?
a: Data arrives with very little delay
More photos fit on the phone
93864.e: Latency is the delay before data reaches its destination. 5G is meant to cut it to a few milliseconds, which is important for remote-controlled machines, for example.
93864.m: Low latency means a short delay.

93865.q: Why do 5G signals with very high frequencies (millimetre waves) only reach a short distance?
a: They are strongly weakened by obstacles
93865.e: Very high frequencies are strongly weakened by walls, trees and even rain. That is why you need lots of small aerials close together for them.
93865.m: The higher the frequency, the shorter the range usually is.

93866.q: What can a modern 5G aerial do so that less energy is lost?
a: Direct the signal towards the phone
93866.e: Modern 5G aerials have many small aerial elements. With them they direct the radio signal like a beam of light towards the device.
93866.m: 5G aerials can direct the signal towards the device.

93867.q: What did the mobile phone companies buy at auction from the federal government in 2019 so that they could offer 5G?
93867.e: Every mobile network needs certain radio frequencies. Switzerland auctioned the frequencies for 5G to the mobile phone companies in 2019.

93868.q: What does Switzerland set for mobile phone aerials to protect people?
a: The number of phones per family
93868.e: A federal ordinance sets limits for the radiation from aerials. Especially strict values apply where people spend a long time.
93868.m: Strict radiation limits apply to mobile phone aerials in Switzerland.

93869.q: What is meant by the “Internet of Things”, which 5G is supposed to promote?
a: Many devices and sensors are connected to the internet
You only buy things on the internet
The internet is printed on paper
93869.e: In the Internet of Things, everyday objects such as sensors, meters or machines are networked. 5G can serve a great many such devices at the same time in one radio cell.
93869.m: In the Internet of Things many objects are networked.

93870.q: What kind of radiation does 5G use for transmission?
93870.e: Like all mobile networks, 5G transmits with electromagnetic waves in the radio frequency range. This radiation is non-ionising, so it cannot ionise atoms.

93871.q: What is the main job of a transmitting aerial?
a: Converting electrical signals into radio waves
93871.e: A transmitting aerial sends out electrical oscillations as electromagnetic waves. A receiving aerial does the opposite and turns radio waves back into electrical signals.
93871.m: Aerials turn electrical signals into radio waves and back.

93873.q: What do you need a satellite dish, which looks like a bowl, for?
93873.e: The curved dish focuses the weak signals of a satellite onto one point. That is where the receiver head sits, which picks up the signals.
93873.m: A satellite dish focuses satellite signals onto one point.

93874.q: How long is the wavelength of a radio wave at 100 megahertz (speed of light about 300,000 km/s)?
93874.e: Wavelength equals the speed of light divided by the frequency: 300,000,000 m/s divided by 100,000,000 Hz gives 3 m.
93874.m: The wavelength is the speed of light divided by the frequency.

93875.q: How is the size of an aerial usually related to the frequency?
a: The higher the frequency, the smaller the aerial
The higher the frequency, the bigger the aerial
93875.e: Aerials are often as long as a fraction of the wavelength, for example half a wavelength. High frequencies have short waves, which is why mobile phone aerials are so small.

93877.q: Why are transmitting aerials often placed on tall towers or mountains?
a: So that the radio waves reach further
So that they use less electricity
So that birds don't disturb them
So that they stay cool in summer
93877.e: Radio waves are blocked by hills and buildings. From a high place they reach a much larger area.
93877.m: High up, radio waves reach further.

93878.q: Why do television aerials on the roof point in a particular direction?
a: Because they receive best from the direction of the transmitter
Because the wind turns them that way
Because all aerials must point north
93878.e: Such roof aerials have several parallel rods. These focus the reception in one direction, so they are pointed at the transmitter.
93878.m: Roof aerials are pointed at the transmitter.

93879.q: Who is the wireless technology Bluetooth named after?
93879.e: The name recalls the Viking king Harald Bluetooth, who united parts of Denmark and Norway in the 10th century. Just as he brought peoples together, Bluetooth is meant to connect devices.
93879.m: Bluetooth is named after King Harald Bluetooth.

93880.q: What is the Bluetooth logo made of?
93880.e: The logo combines the Nordic runes for H and B, the initials of Harald Blåtand. That is why it looks like a pointed B.
93880.m: The Bluetooth logo combines the runes H and B.

93881.q: What kind of connection is Bluetooth mainly intended for?
93881.e: Bluetooth connects devices nearby, such as headphones, keyboards or speakers. Typical ranges are about 10 metres, or more depending on the device.
93881.m: Bluetooth connects devices over short distances.

93882.q: Which other wireless network at home uses similar frequencies to Bluetooth?
93882.e: Bluetooth and Wi-Fi both transmit in the range around 2.4 gigahertz. That is why they can sometimes interfere with each other.
93882.m: Bluetooth and Wi-Fi use similar frequencies.

93883.q: What is it called when two Bluetooth devices are connected for the first time?
93883.e: During pairing two devices get to know each other and exchange a key. After that they connect automatically.
93883.m: When pairing, two Bluetooth devices are linked.

93884.q: Which region do the idea and the name of Bluetooth come from?
93884.e: Bluetooth was developed from 1994 at the Swedish company Ericsson. The name recalls the Danish king Harald Bluetooth.

93885.q: What does “LE” stand for in “Bluetooth LE”?
93885.e: Bluetooth Low Energy uses especially little electricity. That makes it suitable for fitness bands, sensors and devices with small batteries.
93885.m: Bluetooth LE is an especially power-saving version.

93886.q: Why does Bluetooth change its radio frequency very often (frequency hopping)?
a: To avoid interference from other devices
93886.e: Bluetooth jumps between channels many hundreds of times per second. If one channel is disturbed, the signal is soon on another one.
93886.m: Frequency hopping makes Bluetooth less prone to interference.

93887.q: Which device is typically NOT connected via Bluetooth?
a: A fibre optic router to the building's connection
93887.e: Headphones, keyboards and smartwatches often connect via Bluetooth. A router's connection to the building, on the other hand, runs over a cable, such as an optical fibre.
93887.m: Bluetooth replaces short cables between devices close to each other.

93888.e: DAB+ stands for “Digital Audio Broadcasting”. It offers more stations and reception without hiss.

93889.q: Which radio technology is being replaced by DAB+ in Switzerland?
93889.e: Analogue FM radio is being switched off step by step in Switzerland. Today people mainly listen to the radio via DAB+ and the internet.
93889.m: In Switzerland DAB+ is replacing FM radio.

93890.q: When did SRG switch off its FM transmitters?
93890.e: SRG stopped broadcasting its radio programmes on FM on 31 December 2024. Since then its stations can be heard digitally via DAB+ and the internet.
93890.m: SRG ended FM at the end of 2024.

93891.q: What happens to an old FM radio when the FM transmitters are switched off?
a: It no longer receives these stations
93891.e: An FM radio can only receive FM. When the FM transmitters are switched off, you need a DAB+ radio or listen via the internet.
93891.m: Without FM transmitters you need a DAB+ or internet radio.

93892.q: What is an advantage of DAB+ over FM?
a: It also sends pictures in cinema quality
93892.e: With DAB+ many programmes fit into one frequency block, and the sound stays free of hiss. Extra information such as song titles can also be displayed.
93892.m: DAB+ offers more stations and hiss-free sound.

93893.q: What do you need to listen to the radio via DAB+?
a: A radio that can receive DAB+
93893.e: DAB+ is broadcast digitally by radio waves. You need a suitable receiver; many new radios and car radios can do this.
93893.m: For DAB+ you need a DAB+ radio.

93894.q: What does the plus in the name DAB+ mean?
a: It is an improved version of DAB
It only broadcasts temperatures above zero in the weather
It has twice as many aerials
93894.e: DAB+ is the further development of the older DAB. It packs the sound more efficiently, so more stations fit into the same frequency block.
93894.m: DAB+ is the improved version of DAB.

93895.q: What does a DAB+ radio often display in addition to the music?
a: The water temperature of the Rhine
93895.e: As well as sound, DAB+ also transmits short texts. That is why many devices show the station name, the title of the song or traffic information.
93895.m: DAB+ also transmits texts such as the song title.

93896.q: What does streaming mean for music and videos?
a: Playing while the data is still loading
93896.e: When streaming, the data comes continuously from the internet and is played straight away. You don't have to wait until the whole file has downloaded.
93896.m: When streaming, things play while the data flows.

93897.q: What is the temporary store called that loads a few seconds in advance when streaming?
93897.e: The buffer stores a piece of video or music in advance. If there is a short disruption in the network, playback carries on.
93897.m: The buffer bridges short disruptions when streaming.

93898.q: Why are videos compressed for streaming?
a: So that less data has to be sent
So that they become more colourful
93898.e: Uncompressed videos would be huge. Compression methods leave out unnecessary information so that the data fits through the internet.
93898.m: Compression makes video files much smaller.

93899.q: What does the bit rate mean in streaming?
93899.e: The bit rate tells you how many bits are sent per second. A higher bit rate usually means better quality, but more data.
93899.m: The bit rate measures the amount of data per second.

93900.q: Why does a streamed video often become blurrier automatically when the internet is slow?
a: The quality is adjusted to the connection
93900.e: With adaptive streaming the player chooses a suitable quality level depending on the network speed. This way the video keeps playing, just at a lower resolution.
93900.m: Adaptive streaming adjusts the quality to the network.

a: A photo in a photo album
93901.e: In a livestream an event, such as a concert or a match, is broadcast as it happens. Viewers see it with almost no delay.
93901.m: A livestream shows an event in real time.

93902.q: What is the difference between streaming and downloading?
a: With a download the file is saved permanently
With streaming you don't need the internet
Streaming only works on the television
93902.e: After a download the file is on the device and can also be used offline. With streaming it is only loaded temporarily and played.
93902.m: A download stays saved, a stream doesn't.

93903.q: Why do streaming services store copies of their videos on servers in many countries?
a: So that the data has a short way to the viewers
So that the videos become more colourful
So that you no longer need the internet
So that the films last longer
93903.e: If a video is on a server nearby, it arrives faster and more reliably. Such worldwide server networks are called content delivery networks.

a: It turns electrical signals into sound
93904.e: In the loudspeaker the electrical signal moves a membrane. This makes the air vibrate, and we hear sound.
93904.m: A loudspeaker turns electrical signals into sound.

93905.q: Which part moves in the field of a permanent magnet in a dynamic loudspeaker?
93905.e: When alternating current flows through the voice coil, it is pushed back and forth in the magnetic field. The coil is connected to the membrane and moves it too.
93905.m: The voice coil moves the loudspeaker's membrane.

93906.q: What is the loudspeaker called that mainly reproduces low notes (bass)?
93906.e: Woofers have a large membrane that can move a lot of air. Very specialised bass boxes are called subwoofers.
93906.m: A woofer is responsible for the bass.

93907.q: Which part in a speaker box divides the signal between the individual loudspeakers according to pitch?
93907.e: The crossover sends high frequencies to the small loudspeaker for the treble and low ones to the large one. This way each loudspeaker works in its suitable range.
93907.m: The crossover divides the sounds between the loudspeakers.

93908.q: Roughly which frequency range can a young person hear?
93908.e: Young people hear from about 20 hertz to 20 kilohertz. With age, it is mainly the upper limit that drops.
93908.m: We hear sounds from about 20 to 20,000 hertz.

93909.q: What is the minimum number of loudspeakers needed for stereo sound?
93909.e: Stereo has a left and a right channel. This creates the impression that sounds come from different sides.
93909.m: Stereo needs a left and a right loudspeaker.

93910.q: Why are loudspeakers usually built into a cabinet?
a: So that the sound waves produced at the front and back don't cancel each other out
So that they don't get wet
So that they use less electricity
93910.e: The membrane produces opposing sound waves at the front and back, which cancel each other out, especially with low notes. The cabinet separates them; this is called an acoustic short circuit.
93910.m: The cabinet prevents an acoustic short circuit.

93911.q: Which device boosts the weak music signal before it drives the loudspeaker?
93911.e: The signal from a player is too weak for large loudspeakers. An amplifier makes it strong enough for the membrane to move a lot.

a: It turns sound into electrical signals
93912.e: Sound waves make a thin membrane in the microphone vibrate. This movement is turned into an electrical signal.
93912.m: A microphone turns sound into electrical signals.

93913.q: Which device works in principle like a dynamic microphone in reverse?
93913.e: In a dynamic microphone the sound moves a coil in a magnetic field, and a voltage is produced. In a loudspeaker, the other way round, the current moves the coil.
93913.m: Microphone and loudspeaker work on the same principle, just the other way round.

93914.q: What is the loud whistling called when a microphone is too close to a loudspeaker?
93914.e: The loudspeaker plays the sound, the microphone picks it up again, and it is amplified over and over. This creates a shrill whistle.
93914.m: Feedback happens when the microphone hears its own loudspeaker.

93915.q: Which type of microphone needs a power supply, often called “phantom power”?
93915.e: A condenser microphone measures the vibrations using a capacitor, which needs a voltage. In the studio the mixing desk often supplies 48 volts of phantom power.
93915.m: Condenser microphones need their own power supply.

93916.q: What is a microphone called that mainly picks up sound from the front and hardly any from behind?
93916.e: In a diagram, the pickup pattern of a cardioid microphone looks heart-shaped. It mainly records from the front and blocks out noises from behind.
93916.m: A cardioid microphone mainly listens to the front.

93917.q: What is a pop filter in front of a vocal microphone for?
a: It softens bursts of air on sounds like P and B
93917.e: Sounds like P and B produce a strong burst of air that “pops” in the microphone. The pop filter made of fabric or metal slows this burst of air down.
93917.m: A pop filter prevents popping noises.

93918.q: Why does a smartphone often have several tiny microphones?
a: So that the battery lasts longer
93918.e: The microphones sit in different places on the device. By comparing their signals, the smartphone can calculate out background noise.
93918.m: Several microphones help the smartphone against background noise.

93919.q: What is a small microphone called that is clipped to clothing, for example in television interviews?
93919.e: A clip-on microphone, also called a lavalier microphone, is fastened to a shirt or collar with a clip. This leaves the speaker's hands free.
93919.m: A clip-on microphone is fastened to clothing.

93920.q: How many digits does the EAN barcode on most products in shops have?
93920.e: The usual barcode in retail is called EAN-13 and has 13 digits. There is also the short form EAN-8 for small packs.
93920.m: The normal EAN barcode has 13 digits.

93921.q: What is the last digit of an EAN barcode for?
93921.e: The last digit is calculated from all the other digits. This lets the till tell whether the code was read correctly.
93921.m: The check digit detects reading errors in the barcode.

93922.q: Which digits do the barcodes of companies that received their numbers in Switzerland begin with?
93922.e: The organisation GS1 assigns number ranges to each country. Switzerland and Liechtenstein have the prefixes 760 to 769; 400 to 440 belong to Germany.
93922.m: Swiss EAN codes begin with 760 to 769.

93923.q: Why can a scanner tell apart the bars of a barcode?
a: Dark bars reflect less light than light gaps
The bars send out radio waves
93923.e: The scanner lights up the code and measures how much light comes back. Black bars absorb the light, white gaps reflect it.
93923.m: A scanner reads barcodes using reflected light.

93924.q: Which product was the first to be scanned by barcode at a till in the USA in 1974?
93924.e: On 26 June 1974 a packet of chewing gum was scanned in a supermarket in Ohio. This packet is now in a museum.
93924.m: The first scanned product was a packet of chewing gum.

93925.q: What was the invention of the barcode mainly meant to make easier?
a: Quickly recording goods at the till
93925.e: Instead of typing in every price, a scanner reads the code in an instant. The idea was patented in 1952 and caught on in shops from 1974.

93926.q: Which digits does the ISBN barcode on books begin with?
93926.e: The ISBN-13 was built into the EAN system. For this it was given the prefix 978 or 979, which stands for “Bookland”.

93927.q: What is the difference between a barcode and a QR code?
a: A barcode is one-dimensional, a QR code two-dimensional
A QR code can only store numbers
93927.e: A barcode only stores information in one direction, in the width of the bars. A QR code uses height and width and therefore holds much more data.
93927.m: Barcodes are one-dimensional, QR codes two-dimensional.

93928.q: What does “QR” stand for in QR code?
93928.e: QR means “Quick Response”. The code was meant to be especially quick to read.

93929.q: In which country was the QR code invented in 1994?
93929.e: The Japanese company Denso Wave developed the QR code in 1994. It made the technology freely available, which is why anyone can use it today.
93929.m: The QR code comes from Japan.

93930.q: What was the QR code originally developed for?
a: To track car parts in production
93930.e: Denso Wave belongs to the group around the car maker Toyota. The code was meant to make parts quickly recognisable in factories.
93930.m: QR codes were first used for car parts.

93931.q: What are the three large squares in the corners of a QR code for?
a: So that the scanner recognises its position and orientation
For the colour of the code
93931.e: The three position markers show the reader where the code is and how it is turned. This lets you scan it from any angle.
93931.m: The three corner squares show the position of the QR code.

93932.q: Why can a QR code often still be read when part of it is dirty?
93932.e: A QR code stores extra data for error correction. Depending on the level, it can still be read with about 7 to 30 per cent damage.
93932.m: Thanks to error correction a QR code works even when slightly damaged.

93933.q: Which Swiss payment slip with a QR code replaced the old red and orange payment slips?
93933.e: Since 2020 Switzerland has had the QR-bill with the Swiss QR Code. The old payment slips were abolished in autumn 2022.
93933.m: In Switzerland bills are paid with the Swiss QR Code.

93934.q: What is shown in the middle of the Swiss QR Code on the QR-bill?
93934.e: In the centre of the Swiss QR Code there is a small Swiss cross. This shows that it is a payment code.
93934.m: The Swiss QR Code has a Swiss cross in the middle.

93936.q: Why should you be careful with unknown QR codes, for example on parking meters?
a: They can lead to fraudulent websites
They use up all your credit
93936.e: Fraudsters sometimes stick fake QR codes over real ones. These lead to fake sites that try to steal payment details.
93936.m: Check the address before you trust a QR code.

93937.q: What does the abbreviation RFID stand for?
93937.e: RFID means “Radio-Frequency Identification”. Objects or animals are recognised by radio without having to be seen.
93937.m: RFID recognises things with the help of radio waves.

93938.q: Where does a passive RFID chip get its energy from?
93938.e: Passive RFID tags have no battery. The reader creates a field that briefly supplies the chip with energy so that it can reply.
93938.m: Passive RFID chips get their energy from the reader.

93939.q: Where is RFID often used in Swiss ski resorts?
a: In ski passes for the turnstiles
In piste machines as the engine
In snow cannons as the pump
93939.e: Many ski passes contain an RFID chip. The turnstile at the lift recognises the pass even when it is in your jacket pocket.
93939.m: Ski passes open the turnstile by RFID.

93940.q: What must dogs in Switzerland carry under their skin so that they can be identified?
93940.e: In Switzerland every dog must be marked with a microchip. The chip is read by RFID, and the data is registered in a database.
93940.m: Dogs in Switzerland carry an RFID microchip.

93941.q: Which short-range wireless technology, based on RFID, is used for contactless payment with a mobile phone?
93941.e: NFC stands for “Near Field Communication” and only works over a few centimetres. That makes it suitable for payments and access cards.

93942.q: What advantage does RFID have over a barcode?
a: It doesn't need a line of sight
It only works in the dark
93942.e: A barcode has to be visible in front of the scanner. RFID chips are read by radio, even through packaging and several at once.
93942.m: RFID works without a line of sight.

93943.q: What do many libraries use RFID labels in books for?
a: For self-service lending and theft protection
93943.e: With RFID, readers can borrow and return books themselves. At the exit a gate detects books that have not been borrowed.
93943.m: Libraries use RFID for lending and security.

93944.q: What is inside today's Swiss passport?
a: A chip with the passport data
93944.e: Since 2006 the Swiss passport has had a chip that is read contactlessly by radio. Among other things, the photo and fingerprints are stored on it.
93944.m: The Swiss passport contains a radio chip.

94045.q: Which herb is the main ingredient in green pesto?
94045.e: Green pesto is made from basil, pine nuts, cheese, garlic and olive oil. It comes from Italy.
94045.m: Green pesto is made from basil.

94046.q: Which vegetable is basil especially often eaten with?
94046.e: Basil goes very well with tomatoes. For example, people eat tomatoes with mozzarella and basil.

94047.q: Which country's cooking is hard to imagine without basil?
94047.e: In Italy basil goes into many dishes, for example pesto or tomato sauce.
94047.m: Basil is very popular in Italian cooking.

94048.q: What can basil not cope with at all?
94048.e: Basil is a plant from warm regions. Even a frost kills it.
94048.m: Basil likes warmth and cannot cope with frost.

94049.q: Basil is also called the “royal herb”. Where does this name come from?
94049.e: The name basil comes from the Greek word for royal. That is why it is also called the royal herb.
94049.m: Basil is also called the royal herb.

94050.q: Which country does basil probably originally come from?
94050.e: Basil probably comes from India and reached Europe through trade. It needs lots of warmth.

94051.q: Where does basil grow best in the garden or on the balcony?
a: In the water of the pond
94051.e: Basil needs lots of light and warmth. It is best in a sheltered spot in the sun.
94051.m: Basil needs a warm, sunny spot.

94052.q: Which pizza is traditionally topped with tomatoes, mozzarella and basil?
94052.e: Pizza Margherita has the colours red, white and green. The green comes from the basil.
94052.m: Basil belongs on a Pizza Margherita.

94053.q: Which part of basil do people usually eat?
94053.e: With basil, people mainly use the fresh green leaves. They pick them off the plant.
94053.m: We eat the leaves of basil.

94054.q: Which two kinds of parsley can you often buy?
94054.e: Curly parsley has crinkly leaves, flat-leaf parsley has flat leaves. Flat-leaf usually tastes stronger.
94054.m: There is curly and flat-leaf parsley.

94055.q: Which vegetable is parsley related to?
94055.e: Parsley and carrots belong to the same plant family, the carrot family (umbellifers). You can tell by the flowers.
94055.m: Parsley is related to the carrot.

94056.q: Which vitamin is found in especially large amounts in fresh parsley?
94056.e: Fresh parsley contains a lot of vitamin C. That is why it is especially healthy raw.
94056.m: Parsley contains lots of vitamin C.

94057.q: In which year does a parsley plant usually flower?
94057.e: Parsley is a biennial. In the first year it grows leaves, and in the second year it flowers.
94057.m: Parsley flowers in its second year.

94058.q: Which part of parsley is usually sprinkled over food?
94058.e: The fresh green leaves are finely chopped and sprinkled over soups, potatoes or salad.
94058.m: We usually eat the leaves of parsley.

94059.q: Which poisonous plant can be mistaken for flat-leaf parsley?
94059.e: Fool's parsley looks similar to flat-leaf parsley but is poisonous. That is why you should not just pick herbs in the wild.

94060.q: What are boiled potatoes sprinkled with chopped herbs called?
94060.e: Boiled potatoes with butter and chopped parsley are called parsley potatoes. They are a popular side dish.
94060.m: Parsley potatoes are sprinkled with parsley.

94061.q: Which region does parsley originally come from?
94061.e: Parsley comes from the area around the Mediterranean Sea. Today it grows in many gardens.

94062.q: What do the stalks of chives look like?
94062.e: Chives have thin, tube-shaped stalks. They are hollow inside.

94063.q: What is the right way to harvest chives?
a: Cut the stalks off above the ground
94063.e: You cut the stalks with scissors a few centimetres above the ground. New stalks then grow back.
94063.m: Cut chives off above the ground.

94064.e: The flowers are small balls in pink to purple. They look very pretty.
94064.m: Chives have pink to purple flowers.

94065.e: The flowers are edible and taste mildly of onion. You can use them to decorate a salad.

94067.q: What happens to the chives in the garden after the winter?
94067.e: Chives are perennial. In winter they die back and in spring they sprout again.

94068.q: Why are chives usually added to food only at the end?
a: They lose their flavour when cooked
94068.e: Chives taste best fresh. If you cook them, their flavour is lost.
94068.m: Chives go fresh on the finished food.

94069.q: Where do chives also grow wild in Switzerland?
94069.e: Wild chives grow in the Alps, for example in damp spots in mountain meadows.
94069.m: Chives grow wild in the Alps.

94070.q: Which popular drink is made from peppermint leaves?
94070.e: You pour hot water over the leaves. This makes peppermint tea, hot or cold.

94071.q: Which substance makes peppermint feel cool in your mouth?
94071.e: Peppermint contains menthol. It gives a cool, fresh feeling in your mouth.
94071.m: The menthol in peppermint has a cooling effect.

94072.q: What does toothpaste often taste of?
94072.e: Many toothpastes taste of mint. That gives you fresh breath.

94073.q: How does peppermint spread in the garden?
a: With long runners in the ground
It does not spread at all
94073.e: Peppermint forms long runners under the ground. This way it quickly grows in all directions.

94074.q: What does peppermint feel like in your mouth?
94074.e: Peppermint contains a substance that feels cool in your mouth. That is why peppermint tea and peppermint sweets taste so fresh.
94074.m: Peppermint feels fresh and cool in your mouth.

94075.q: What shape is the stem of peppermint?
94075.e: If you roll the stem between your fingers, you can feel four edges. That is typical of mints.
94075.m: The peppermint stem has four edges.

a: It tastes strong and a bit hot
It is red like chilli peppers
94076.e: Peppermint tastes strong and a little bit hot. That is why it got the name pepper.

94077.q: Which kind of soil does peppermint like best?
94077.e: Mints like to grow in damp places. In the garden you need to water them regularly.

94078.q: Which part of peppermint is used for tea?
94078.e: For tea you use the fresh or dried leaves. That is where the fresh flavour is.
94078.m: Peppermint tea is made from the leaves.

94079.e: Thyme has tiny leaves on thin twigs. You strip them off with your fingers.

94080.q: What happens to thyme stems as the plant gets older?
94080.e: Thyme is a small shrubby plant. At the bottom, its twigs become hard and woody over time.

94081.q: Which region does common thyme come from?
94081.e: Common thyme comes from the warm countries around the Mediterranean. There it grows on dry slopes.

94082.q: What is thyme tea often drunk for?
94082.e: Thyme is an old medicinal plant. Thyme tea is traditionally drunk for a cough.
94082.m: Thyme tea is often drunk for a cough.

94083.q: Which animals like to visit thyme flowers?
94083.e: Thyme has lots of small flowers full of nectar. Bees, bumblebees and butterflies love to fly there.

94084.q: What kind of spot does thyme like?
94084.e: Thyme loves lots of sun and dry soil. Too much water harms it.
94084.m: Thyme likes it sunny and dry.

94085.q: Which kind of thyme smells of a sour citrus fruit?
94085.e: Lemon thyme has a fresh lemony smell. People like to use it for fish or tea.

94086.q: Which food does thyme go well with?
94086.e: Thyme gives tomato sauce, meat and potatoes a strong flavour. It is a typical kitchen herb.
94086.m: Thyme goes well with savoury dishes.

94087.q: What colour are the flowers of common thyme usually?
94087.e: Thyme has lots of tiny flowers in pale purple, pink or white. They appear in early summer.
94087.m: Thyme usually has pale purple to pink flowers.

94088.q: What do rosemary leaves look like?
94088.e: Rosemary has narrow, leathery leaves. They look a bit like fir needles.

94089.q: Which region does rosemary come from?
94089.e: Rosemary grows wild on the coasts of the Mediterranean. It loves sun and warmth.

94090.q: What is often seasoned with rosemary before it goes in the oven?
94090.e: Roast potatoes with rosemary are very popular. The rosemary gives them a spicy smell.
94090.m: Rosemary goes well with roast potatoes.

94091.q: What happens to rosemary leaves in winter?
94091.e: Rosemary is evergreen. It keeps its leaves in winter too.

94092.q: What colour are rosemary flowers usually?
94092.e: Rosemary has small, usually light blue flowers. They appear as early as spring.
94092.m: Rosemary usually has light blue flowers.

94093.q: What does a rosemary plant in Switzerland often need in winter?
94093.e: Rosemary comes from warm countries. In hard frost you should protect it or keep it indoors somewhere bright and cool over winter.
94093.m: Rosemary must be protected from hard frost.

94094.q: What does the Latin name “ros marinus” mean?
94094.e: “Ros marinus” means dew of the sea. Rosemary often grows close to the sea.
94094.m: Rosemary means dew of the sea.

94095.q: What kind of plant is rosemary?
94095.e: Rosemary grows as a shrub with woody twigs. It can grow more than a metre tall.

94096.q: How much water does rosemary in a pot need?
a: It has to stand in water
94096.e: Rosemary comes from dry regions. Too much water makes its roots rot.

94097.q: What do the leaves of common sage feel like?
94097.e: Sage leaves have fine hairs. That is why they feel velvety and look grey-green.

94098.q: What is sage tea traditionally often used for?
a: For gargling when you have a sore throat
94098.e: Sage is an old medicinal plant. People traditionally gargle with sage tea when their throat is scratchy.
94098.m: Gargle with sage tea for a sore throat.

94099.q: What are sage leaves fried in batter called in Switzerland, because their stalk looks like a mouse's tail?
94099.e: For Müslichüechli, sage leaves are dipped in batter and fried in hot fat. The stalk looks like a mouse's tail.

94100.q: Which Italian meat dish is made with sage and cured ham?
94100.e: For saltimbocca, sage and cured ham are laid on a thin veal escalope. The name means “jump into the mouth”.

94101.q: The name sage comes from the Latin word “salvare”. What does it mean?
94101.e: “Salvare” means to heal or to save. Sage was known early on as a medicinal plant.

94102.q: Which plant family does sage belong to?
94102.e: Sage belongs to the mint family, also called the lipped flowers. Its flowers look like little open lips.
94102.m: Sage belongs to the mint family.

94103.q: What colour are the flowers of common sage usually?
94103.e: Common sage has bluish purple flowers in early summer. Lots of insects visit the flowers.
94103.m: Common sage has bluish purple flowers.

94104.q: With which sauce do people like to eat gnocchi together with sage?
94104.e: Sage leaves are fried in butter until it turns brown. This sage butter goes well with gnocchi or ravioli.
94104.m: Sage butter goes well with gnocchi.

94105.q: What do dill leaves look like?
94105.e: Dill has very fine, thread-like leaves. They look almost like feathers.
94105.m: Dill has leaves as fine as threads.

94107.q: Which food does dill go especially well with?
94107.e: Dill and fish go very well together. Salmon with dill, for example, is well known.

94108.e: Dill flowers in large, flat umbrella-like clusters with lots of small yellow flowers.

94109.q: Apart from the leaves, which part of dill is also used as a spice?
94109.e: Dill seeds are a spice. They are used, for example, in bread or pickled vegetables.
94109.m: Dill seeds are a spice too.

94110.q: How long does a dill plant live?
94110.e: Dill is an annual. You sow it again every year.
94110.m: Dill has to be sown again every year.

94111.q: In which part of Europe is dill especially popular in cooking?
94111.e: In Sweden, Norway and Finland, dill goes into many dishes. It is popular there with fish and potatoes.
94111.m: People eat a lot of dill in Scandinavia.

94112.q: When is the best time to add fresh dill to food?
a: Right at the start of cooking
94112.e: Fresh dill loses its flavour if it is cooked for a long time. That is why you sprinkle it over only at the end.
94112.m: Add fresh dill only at the end.

94113.q: What do the flowers of German chamomile look like?
94113.e: The flowers have white petals around a yellow centre. They look like little stars.
94113.m: Chamomile flowers are white with a yellow centre.

94114.q: What is chamomile tea traditionally often drunk for?
94114.e: Chamomile tea is an old home remedy. Many people traditionally drink it when they have a tummy ache.
94114.m: Chamomile tea is often drunk for a tummy ache.

94115.q: Which part of chamomile is used for tea?
94115.e: For chamomile tea you use the dried flower heads. That is where the typical scent is.

94116.q: How can you recognise German chamomile when you cut through the yellow centre?
94116.e: In German chamomile, the yellow flower base is hollow inside. In similar plants it is filled.
94116.m: German chamomile has a hollow flower centre.

94117.q: Where does German chamomile often grow wild?
94117.e: German chamomile likes to grow in fields and along the edges of paths. It likes sun.

94118.q: Which flower does chamomile look like?
94118.e: Chamomile and daisies both have white petals and a yellow centre. They belong to the same plant family.

94119.q: In which season does chamomile mainly flower?
94119.e: Chamomile mainly flowers from May into the summer. That is when people collect the flowers.

94120.q: What do people traditionally do with hot chamomile tea when they have a cold?
94120.e: You lean over a bowl of hot chamomile tea and breathe in the steam. This is called inhaling.
94120.m: With a cold, people inhale chamomile steam.

94121.q: What do the leaves of lemon balm smell of?
94121.e: When you rub the leaves, they smell fresh and lemony. That is why the plant has its name.

94122.q: The word “Melissa”, the scientific name of lemon balm, comes from Greek. What does it mean?
94122.e: In Greek, “mélissa” means honeybee. Bees love to fly to the flowers of this plant.
94122.m: Melissa is the Greek word for honeybee.

94123.q: When is lemon balm tea traditionally drunk?
a: In the morning to wake up
94123.e: Lemon balm tea has long been thought to be calming. That is why many people drink it in the evening.
94123.m: Lemon balm tea is popular in the evening.

94124.q: Which herb do lemon balm leaves look like?
94124.e: The leaves are egg-shaped with toothed edges, similar to mint. You can tell the difference by the smell.

94125.q: Is lemon balm related to the lemon tree?
a: No, only the smell is similar
Yes, it is a cutting of it
94125.e: Lemon balm is a herb from the mint family. It only happens to smell similar to lemons.
94125.m: Lemon balm is not related to the lemon.

94126.q: What happens to lemon balm in the garden after the winter?
94126.e: Lemon balm is perennial. The top dies back in winter and it grows again in spring.
94126.m: Lemon balm grows back every spring.

94127.q: What colour are the small flowers of lemon balm?
94127.e: Lemon balm has small white to pale pink flowers. They sit where the leaves grow from the stem.
94127.m: Lemon balm has small white flowers.

94128.q: What do people like to use fresh lemon balm for in summer?
94128.e: A few lemon balm leaves make water, iced tea or lemonade nice and fresh.
94128.m: Lemon balm goes well in cold drinks.

94129.q: What colour are lavender flowers usually?
94129.e: Lavender usually flowers purple to blue. That is why this colour is also called lavender.

94130.q: Which region of France has famous lavender fields?
94130.e: In Provence in the south of France, huge purple lavender fields bloom in summer.
94130.m: Provence is famous for its lavender.

94131.q: Why do people put little bags of lavender in the wardrobe?
94131.e: Moths do not like the smell of lavender. That is why people put lavender bags with their clothes.

94132.q: The name lavender may come from the Latin “lavare”. What does that mean?
94132.e: “Lavare” means to wash. People like to put lavender in bath water or in soap.

94133.q: What do lavender leaves look like?
94133.e: Lavender has narrow leaves with a grey sheen. Fine hairs protect them from the heat.

94134.q: Which insects like to collect nectar from lavender flowers?
94134.e: Lavender flowers have lots of sweet nectar. That is why lots of bees and bumblebees buzz around the plant.

94135.q: What is lavender oil made from?
94135.e: Lavender oil is made from the scented flowers. It is used, for example, in soap.
94135.m: Lavender oil comes from the flowers.

94136.q: What kind of spot does lavender like?
94136.e: Lavender needs lots of sun and fairly dry soil. It does not like wet feet.
94136.m: Lavender needs sun and dry soil.

94137.q: Which well-known dish do people often sprinkle oregano on?
94137.e: Oregano is a typical pizza herb. It goes well with tomatoes and cheese.
94137.m: Oregano is a typical pizza herb.

94138.q: What does oregano smell like when you rub a leaf between your fingers?
94138.e: Oregano has a strong, spicy smell. That is why it is used to season pizza and tomato sauce.

94139.q: Which other kitchen herb is oregano closely related to?
94139.e: Oregano and marjoram belong to the same genus. That is why they taste similar.

94140.q: How is oregano especially often used in cooking?
94140.e: Dried oregano has a very strong flavour. That is why it is often used dried.

94141.q: Where does oregano grow wild in Switzerland?
94141.e: Wild oregano grows on sunny slopes and in dry meadows. There it smells strongly in summer.
94141.m: Wild oregano grows in sunny meadows.

94142.q: What colour are oregano flowers usually?
94142.e: Oregano has small pink to pale purple flowers. Butterflies and bees like to visit them.

94143.q: Which sauce do people like to add oregano to?
94143.e: Oregano gives tomato sauce a spicy flavour. It goes into many Italian sauces.
94143.m: Oregano goes well in tomato sauce.

94144.q: How long does an oregano plant live?
94144.e: Oregano is perennial. It grows back every year from the same rootstock.

94145.e: The Swiss engineer Georges de Mestral developed the hook and loop fastener. He called his invention Velcro.

94146.q: Where did the burrs get caught after Georges de Mestral went for a walk?
94146.e: After walks, lots of burrs were stuck in his dog's fur. He wanted to know why they held on so well.
94146.m: The burrs were caught in his dog's fur.

94147.q: What did Georges de Mestral use to look very closely at the burrs?
94147.e: Under the microscope he saw how the burrs hold on to fur and fabric. That is how he got the idea.
94147.m: A microscope makes tiny things look big.

94148.q: What does one side of a Velcro strip have so that it holds?
94148.e: One side has lots of tiny, bendy hooks. They catch on the other side.
94148.m: Velcro holds with lots of tiny hooks.

94149.q: The name “Velcro” contains the French word “velours”. What does “velours” mean?
94149.e: “Velours” means velvet. The soft side of a Velcro strip is a bit like velvet.
94149.m: Velours is the French word for velvet.

94150.q: How did the Swiss Georges de Mestral get the idea for Velcro?
a: Small plant seed heads got caught in his dog's fur
He watched a spider building its web
He watched a woodpecker on a tree
He saw frost patterns on a window
94150.e: After a walk, burrs were stuck in his dog's fur. Under the microscope he saw tiny hooks and copied them. In 1951 he applied for a patent for Velcro.
94150.m: Velcro was copied from the burr.

94151.q: Why do many children's shoes have Velcro?
a: You can do them up quickly without laces
It makes them glow in the dark
94151.e: With Velcro you do not have to tie shoelaces. That is easier for small children.
94151.m: Velcro makes putting on shoes easy.

94152.q: What do astronauts in space need Velcro strips for?
a: So things do not float away
94152.e: In space everything floats around. With Velcro strips you can fix objects to walls or clothes.
94152.m: In space, Velcro strips hold things in place.

94153.q: What colour is the handle of a Swiss Army knife usually?
94153.e: Most everyday Swiss Army knives have a red handle. This makes them well known all over the world.
94153.m: The typical Swiss Army knife has a red handle.

94154.q: Which symbol can be seen on many Swiss Army knives?
94154.e: The white Swiss cross is often shown on the handle. It shows that the knife comes from Switzerland.
94154.m: The Swiss cross can be seen on many pocket knives.

94155.q: Who was the first Swiss Army knife made for?
94155.e: The Swiss Army wanted a practical knife for its soldiers. That is how the first soldier's knife came about in 1890.
94155.m: The first Swiss Army knife was a soldier's knife.

94156.q: Which well-known company grew out of Karl Elsener's knife workshop in Ibach?
94156.e: Karl Elsener made soldier's knives in Ibach from 1891. His workshop became the company Victorinox.
94156.m: Victorinox makes the Swiss Army knife.

94157.q: In which canton is Ibach, where pocket knives are still made today?
94157.e: Ibach is part of the municipality of Schwyz in the canton of Schwyz. Knives have been made there for over 130 years.
94157.m: Ibach is in the canton of Schwyz.

94158.q: The knife company Victorinox is named after Victoria. Who was Victoria?
94158.e: Victoria was the first name of Karl Elsener's mother. He named his brand after her.
94158.m: Victorinox is named after the founder's mother.

94159.q: What does “inox” mean in the name Victorinox?
94159.e: “Inox” is an international word for stainless steel. The blades are made of it.

94160.q: Which tool did the very first Swiss soldier's knife of 1890 already have?
94160.e: The first model had a blade, a tin opener, a screwdriver and an awl. A saw was only added much later.
94160.m: Even the first soldier's knife had a tin opener.

94161.q: Which tool on a pocket knife do you use to pull the cork out of a bottle?
94161.e: The corkscrew is a small spiral. You twist it into the cork and pull it out.
94161.m: You open bottles with corks using the corkscrew.

94162.q: Who invented milk chocolate in Switzerland?
94162.e: Daniel Peter mixed chocolate with milk. That is how Swiss milk chocolate came about.

94163.q: Which milk did Daniel Peter finally use for his chocolate?
94163.e: Fresh milk contains a lot of water, and that does not go well with chocolate. It worked with condensed milk.

94164.q: Which friend helped Daniel Peter with his first experiments with milk?
94164.e: Henri Nestlé was a friend of Daniel Peter. He helped him with his milk powder in the first experiments.
94164.m: Henri Nestlé helped Daniel Peter with his experiments.

94165.q: Which beans is chocolate made from?
94165.e: Chocolate is made from the seeds of the cocoa tree. They are called cocoa beans.
94165.m: Chocolate is made from cocoa beans.

94166.q: Daniel Peter married into a chocolate family. What was the family called?
94166.e: Daniel Peter married Fanny-Louise Cailler. Her father made chocolate.
94166.m: Daniel Peter married into the Cailler family.

94167.q: Which Swiss man invented milk chocolate in 1875?
94167.e: Daniel Peter from Vevey mixed cocoa with milk and, after many attempts, managed to make solid chocolate from it. Rudolf Lindt, on the other hand, invented conching for smooth chocolate.

94168.q: On which lake did Daniel Peter make his first milk chocolate?
94168.e: Daniel Peter came from the canton of Vaud and worked in Vevey on Lake Geneva. His milk chocolate was created there in 1875.
94168.m: Milk chocolate was created on Lake Geneva.

94169.q: What shape are the pieces of a Toblerone?
94169.e: A Toblerone is made of triangles lined up in a row. This shape has been protected since 1909.

94170.q: In which Swiss city was Toblerone invented?
94170.e: Toblerone was invented in the Swiss capital. The first factory is there too.

94171.q: In which year was Toblerone invented?
94171.e: Toblerone has existed since 1908. So it is more than 100 years old.

94172.q: Who invented Toblerone together with Emil Baumann?
94172.e: Theodor Tobler and Emil Baumann invented Toblerone. That is why the name begins with “Tobler”.

94173.q: The name Toblerone contains the Italian word “torrone”. What is torrone?
a: A nougat made of honey and almonds
94173.e: Torrone is a sweet nougat made of honey and almonds. There are little pieces of it in the chocolate.
94173.m: Torrone is a nougat made of honey and almonds.

94174.q: Which Swiss mountain could be seen on the Toblerone packaging for a long time?
94174.e: For a long time the packaging showed the Matterhorn. Since 2023 a different, made-up mountain has been shown there.
94174.m: For a long time the Matterhorn was on the Toblerone packaging.

94175.q: Which animal is hidden in the mountain on the Toblerone packaging?
94175.e: If you look closely, you will find the outline of a bear in the mountain. Many people only spot it after searching for a long time.
94175.m: A bear is hidden in the Toblerone mountain.

94176.q: In which country has Toblerone partly been made since 2023?
94176.e: Since 2023, some Toblerone has been made in Bratislava in Slovakia. That is why the packaging may no longer show a Swiss mountain.
94176.m: Toblerone is partly made in Slovakia.

94177.q: Which kinds of chocolate does Toblerone come in?
94177.e: Toblerone comes in milk chocolate, dark chocolate and white chocolate. All of them contain nougat.
94177.m: Toblerone comes in several kinds of chocolate.

94178.q: In which year did the first Swatch come onto the market?
94178.e: The first Swatch was presented on 1 March 1983. It helped the Swiss watch industry through a difficult time.

94179.q: What material is the case of a classic Swatch made of?
94179.e: The classic Swatch has a plastic case. That is why it is light and cheap.
94179.m: The classic Swatch is made of plastic.

94180.q: Which two English words did the name Swatch come from?
94180.e: Swatch is short for “Second Watch”. You were meant to be able to change it like a piece of clothing.

94181.q: Who is seen as the “father of the Swatch”?
94181.e: Nicolas G. Hayek made the Swatch big and famous. It was designed by engineers at the company ETA.
94181.m: Nicolas G. Hayek is seen as the father of the Swatch.

94182.q: Which country do Swatch watches come from?
94182.e: Swatch is a watch brand from Switzerland. The company has its headquarters in Biel.

94183.q: In which city was the Swatch presented for the first time?
94183.e: The Swatch was shown for the first time in Zurich in 1983. After that it quickly became very popular.
94183.m: The Swatch was presented in Zurich.

94184.q: What are Swatch watches especially known for?
94184.e: Swatch watches come in lots of cheerful colours and patterns. Some were designed by artists.

94185.q: What do you usually do with Ovomaltine powder?
94185.e: Ovomaltine is a powder that you stir into milk. This makes a sweet drink.

94186.q: In which year did Ovomaltine come onto the market?
94186.e: Ovomaltine has existed since 1904. At first it was sold as a strengthening drink.

94187.e: The chemist Albert Wander developed Ovomaltine. His father had founded the Wander company.

94188.q: Which ingredient makes up most of Swiss Ovomaltine?
94188.e: Swiss Ovomaltine is about two thirds barley malt extract (as of 2024). That is where the “malt” part of the name comes from.

94189.q: The “Ovo” in the name comes from the Latin word “ovum”. What does it mean?
94189.e: “Ovum” is Latin for egg. Ovomaltine used to contain eggs too.
94189.m: Ovum is the Latin word for egg.

94190.q: What is Ovomaltine called in England and the USA?
94190.e: In England, the USA and many other countries it is called Ovaltine. The recipe there is a little different.
94190.m: In English-speaking countries Ovomaltine is called Ovaltine.

94191.q: In which place in the canton of Bern is Ovomaltine made today?
94191.e: The Wander company makes Ovomaltine in Neuenegg in the canton of Bern (as of 2024).

94192.q: In which city did Georg Wander found the company that Ovomaltine came from?
94192.e: Georg Wander founded the company in the federal city of Bern. His son later developed Ovomaltine there.
94192.m: The Wander company was founded in Bern.

94193.e: The doctor Maximilian Bircher-Benner invented muesli around 1900. That is why it is called Bircher muesli.

94194.q: What job did the inventor of Bircher muesli have?
94194.e: Bircher-Benner was a doctor. He wanted his patients to eat healthily, with lots of fruit.
94194.m: The inventor of Bircher muesli was a doctor.

94195.q: Which fruit is the most important ingredient in the original Bircher muesli?
94195.e: In the original recipe, lots of sour apples were grated, skin and all. The apple was the main thing.
94195.m: Apple is the main ingredient in the original Bircher muesli.

94196.q: Which flakes belong in Bircher muesli?
94196.e: Bircher muesli contains soaked oat flakes. In the original there was only one spoonful of them.
94196.m: Oat flakes belong in Bircher muesli.

94197.q: What do you stir into the flakes so that Bircher muesli becomes nice and moist?
94197.e: For Bircher muesli you soak oat flakes and stir in milk or yoghurt. Then grated apples are added.
94197.m: Milk or yoghurt goes into Bircher muesli.

94198.q: What does the Swiss German word “Müesli” mean?
94198.e: “Müesli” is the diminutive of “Mues”. Mues is a soft mush, like a purée.

94199.q: In which city did Bircher-Benner serve muesli in his sanatorium?
94199.e: Bircher-Benner had his clinic in Zurich. From 1904 he ran a sanatorium on the Zürichberg.
94199.m: Bircher-Benner had his sanatorium in Zurich.

94200.q: What was sprinkled on top of the original Bircher muesli?
94200.e: To finish, a spoonful of grated hazelnuts, walnuts or almonds went on top.
94200.m: Grated nuts went on top of the original Bircher muesli.

94201.q: Which country does the well-known Rex peeler come from?
94201.e: The Rex was invented in Switzerland in 1947. It is still made in almost the same way today.
94201.m: The Rex peeler is a Swiss design classic.

94203.q: The well-known Swiss vegetable peeler is called Rex. How does its blade lie?
94203.e: On the Rex, the blade lies across the handle and can move. That way it adapts to the shape of potatoes and carrots.
94203.m: On the Rex, the blade lies across the handle.

94204.q: What was the Rex peeler pictured on in 2003?
94204.e: In 2003, Swiss Post issued a stamp showing the Rex. It was part of a series on Swiss design classics.
94204.m: The Rex was on a stamp in 2003.

94205.q: In which place in the canton of Zurich was the Rex made for decades by the company Zena?
94205.e: The company Zena from Affoltern am Albis made the Rex for decades. Since 2020, Zena has belonged to Victorinox.
94205.m: The Rex was made in Affoltern am Albis for a long time.

94206.q: Which country did Julius Maggi, who invented the stock cube, come from?
94206.e: Julius Maggi was a Swiss businessman. He invented soups, seasoning and the stock cube.

94207.q: In which canton was Julius Maggi's factory?
94207.e: In 1869 Julius Maggi took over a mill in Kemptthal near Winterthur in the canton of Zurich. His factory grew up there.
94207.m: The Maggi factory was in Kemptthal in the canton of Zurich.

94208.q: What do you need a stock cube for?
94208.e: A stock cube contains spices and salt in solid form. With it you can quickly make a stock.
94208.m: With a stock cube you can quickly make a soup.

94209.q: What do you add to a stock cube to make stock?
94209.e: The cube dissolves in hot water. That turns it into stock.
94209.m: A stock cube dissolves in hot water.

94210.q: What did Julius Maggi invent in 1886 to make his soups taste better?
94210.e: In 1886 Maggi brought out his liquid seasoning. It still comes in a brown bottle today.
94210.m: Julius Maggi invented a liquid seasoning in 1886.

94211.q: What did Julius Maggi make his first ready-made soups from?
94211.e: Maggi made cheap soups from the flour of pulses such as peas and beans. They were nourishing and cheap.
94211.m: The first Maggi soups were made from pulses.

94212.q: In which town was Julius Maggi born in 1846?
94212.e: Julius Maggi was born in 1846 in Frauenfeld in the canton of Thurgau.
94212.m: Julius Maggi was born in Frauenfeld.

94213.q: Roughly when did the Maggi stock cube come onto the market?
94213.e: The Maggi stock cube came onto the market shortly after 1900, around 1907 to 1908. So it is more than 100 years old.
94213.m: The Maggi cube has existed for over 100 years.

94214.e: Wim Ouboter from Zurich developed the folding Micro scooter. He founded his own company for it.
94214.m: Wim Ouboter invented the Micro scooter.

94215.q: Which journeys is a scooter especially handy for?
94215.e: On a scooter you are faster than on foot over short distances. It is not made for long journeys.
94215.m: A scooter is meant for short trips.

94216.q: In which country was the folding Micro scooter invented?
94216.e: The Micro scooter was invented in Zurich. Today children all over the world ride it.
94216.m: The Micro scooter comes from Switzerland.

94217.q: What is handy about the Micro scooter?
94217.e: You can fold up the Micro scooter. That way you can easily carry it or take it on the tram.
94217.m: A Micro scooter can be folded up.

94218.q: What material is the frame of a Micro scooter usually made of?
