94218.e: The frame is usually made of aluminium. The metal is light but still strong.
94218.m: Micro scooters usually have an aluminium frame.

94219.q: What should you wear on your head when riding a scooter?
94219.e: A helmet protects your head if you fall. That is why you wear one on a scooter too.
94219.m: A helmet protects your head when you ride a scooter.

94220.q: How do you move forwards on a scooter?
a: You push off with one foot
94220.e: You stand with one foot on the board. With the other foot you push off from the ground.
94220.m: On a scooter you push off with your foot.

94221.q: Which country does the well-known Micro kick scooter come from?
94221.e: The Swiss Wim Ouboter invented the Micro scooter in the 1990s. Around the year 2000, lots of children all over the world wanted one.
94221.m: The Micro kick scooter is a Swiss invention.

a: The coffee powder dissolves in water
94222.e: Nescafé is instant coffee. You put the powder into hot water and have coffee straight away.

94223.e: Nescafé was developed by the company Nestlé in Vevey. Today it is one of the biggest food companies in the world.
94223.m: Nescafé comes from the company Nestlé.

94224.q: Which two words make up the name “Nescafé”?
94224.e: The name combines the company name with the French word “café” for coffee.
94224.m: Nescafé is a short word made from Nestlé and café.

94225.q: What is special about Nescafé from Nestlé?
a: It is coffee powder that dissolves in hot water
It is made from cocoa beans
94225.e: Nescafé is instant coffee. You put the powder into hot water and have a coffee straight away. It came onto the market in 1938.

94226.q: Which country asked Nestlé for help with its coffee in 1930?
94226.e: A great deal of coffee is grown in Brazil. The country was looking for a way to make coffee keep for a long time.
94226.m: Brazil asked Nestlé for help with its coffee.

94227.q: What problem did Brazil have with its coffee around 1930?
a: There was far too much coffee
A disease had destroyed almost all the plants
It had not rained for years
Nobody wanted to grow coffee any more
94227.e: There was so much coffee that the leftovers were burnt or dumped in the sea. People were looking for a way to make coffee keep for a long time.
94227.m: Around 1930 Brazil had too much coffee.

94228.q: In which town on Lake Geneva does the company Nestlé have its headquarters?
94228.e: Nestlé has its headquarters in Vevey on Lake Geneva. Nescafé was also developed there.
94228.m: Nestlé has its headquarters in Vevey.

94229.q: In which country was Nescafé sold for the very first time?
94229.e: The instant coffee first went on sale in shops in Switzerland. After that it was sold in many countries.
94229.m: Nescafé was first sold in Switzerland.

94230.q: What is a coffee creamer lid?
a: The lid of a small portion of cream
94230.e: Coffee cream comes in small pots for one cup of coffee. On top there is a thin lid.
94230.m: A coffee creamer lid seals a small portion of cream.

94231.q: What material is a coffee creamer lid made of?
94231.e: The lid is a very thin foil made of aluminium. It is only about 0.03 to 0.04 millimetres thick.
94231.m: Coffee creamer lids are made of aluminium.

94232.q: What do many people in Switzerland do with coffee creamer lids?
a: They stick them on letters as stamps
They hang them on the Christmas tree
They pay with them in shops
94232.e: The lids have nice pictures and are collected. At swap meets, collectors swap their lids.
94232.m: Many people collect coffee creamer lids.

94233.q: What is often pictured on coffee creamer lids?
94233.e: Every year hundreds of new series with pictures come out. There are, for example, animals, flowers, cars and sights.
94233.m: There are lots of different pictures on coffee creamer lids.

94235.q: Roughly how many coffee creamer lid collectors are there in Switzerland?
94235.e: According to estimates, there are around 30,000 collectors in Switzerland. Switzerland is the centre of this hobby.
94235.m: Many thousands of people in Switzerland collect lids.

94236.q: Since roughly when has coffee cream come in small portion pots?
94236.e: Around 1970, people started filling coffee cream into small pots with an aluminium lid. Soon afterwards, people began to collect them.
94236.m: Portion pots of coffee cream have existed since about 1970.

94237.q: Why does a coffee creamer lid have a small tab?
a: So you can pull it off easily
So it does not blow away
So you can hang it up
94237.e: You can hold the lid by the small tab. That way you can simply pull it off the pot.
94237.m: You pull the lid off by the tab.

94238.q: Where in the nose are the cells that recognise smells?
a: Right at the top of the nose
At the tip of the nose
94238.e: The smell cells are in the lining right at the top of the nasal cavity. That is why you sniff, to pull air upwards.
94238.m: The smell cells are at the top of the nose.

94239.q: Where do the smell cells send their message?
94239.e: The smell cells send signals along nerves to the brain. Only there do we notice what we smell.
94239.m: The brain recognises what the nose smells.

94240.q: Which animal can smell much better than a person?
94240.e: Dogs have many more smell cells than people. That is why they can sniff out trails.
94240.m: Dogs have a very fine nose.

94241.q: What do avalanche dogs in Switzerland search for with their noses?
94241.e: Avalanche dogs smell people lying under the snow. That way they help with rescues in the mountains.
94241.m: Avalanche dogs find buried people with their noses.

94242.q: What does a snake do with its forked tongue?
94242.e: The snake catches scent particles from the air with its tongue. A special organ in its mouth then recognises the smell.
94242.m: Snakes smell with the help of their tongue.

94243.q: What happens if you are around the same smell for a long time?
a: You hardly smell it any more
You smell it more and more strongly
94243.e: The nose gets used to a smell that stays for a long time. That is why you hardly notice the smell of your own home.
94243.m: The nose gets used to smells that stay the same.

94244.q: Which animal helps to find truffles in the ground?
94244.e: Truffles are mushrooms under the ground. Pigs and specially trained dogs can smell them through the soil.
94244.m: Pigs can smell truffles under the ground.

94245.q: What is the sense we use to notice smells called?
94245.e: With our sense of smell we notice scents and stinks. It is one of our five senses.
94245.m: We notice smells with our sense of smell.

94246.q: Why do homes need smoke alarms?
a: When asleep you hardly smell smoke
Smoke smells of nothing at all
Smoke alarms put out the fire
94246.e: Someone who is asleep is usually not woken by the smell of smoke. But the loud alarm of the smoke alarm wakes you up.
94246.m: When you are asleep, the smoke alarm warns you instead of your nose.

94247.q: What have you got when your nose is runny and blocked?
94247.e: With a cold, the inside of the nose is inflamed. It makes a lot of mucus and swells up.
94247.m: With a cold, your nose runs or gets blocked.

94248.q: What usually causes an ordinary cold?
94248.e: A cold is usually caused by viruses. They are passed on when people sneeze, for example.
94248.m: A cold is mostly caused by viruses.

94249.q: Where does a used tissue belong?
94249.e: There are germs in a used tissue. That is why you throw it away and wash your hands afterwards.
94249.m: A used tissue goes in the bin.

94250.q: How long does an ordinary cold usually last?
94250.e: A simple cold usually goes away by itself after about a week.
94250.m: A cold usually goes away after about a week.

94251.q: What helps so that you do not pass your cold on to others?
94251.e: Germs often stick to our hands. We wash them away with water and soap.
94251.m: Washing your hands protects against infection.

94252.q: Does an antibiotic help against an ordinary cold?
a: Yes, straight away after an hour
Yes, but only in the evening
Yes, if you rub it on your nose
94252.e: Antibiotics only work against bacteria. An ordinary cold goes away by itself without them.
94252.m: Antibiotics do not help against an ordinary cold.

a: A cold that only happens in winter
94253.e: With hay fever, the body reacts to the dust from flowers, which is called pollen. Your nose runs and your eyes itch.
94253.m: Hay fever is an allergy to pollen.

94254.q: What does you good when you have a cold?
a: Lots of ice cream and running
94254.e: With a cold, rest and plenty to drink help, for example warm tea. That way the body can recover.
94254.m: With a cold, rest and warm drinks help.

94255.q: What should you never put into a nostril?
94255.e: Small things like beads or peas can get stuck in the nose. Then a doctor often has to help.
94255.m: Small objects do not belong in the nose.

94256.q: What are the two openings in a horse's nose called?
94256.e: Horses and cattle breathe through their nostrils. They can open them very wide.
94256.m: Horses can open their nostrils wide.

94257.q: Which animal has its nostrils at the tip of a long trunk?
94257.e: An elephant's trunk is a very long nose. Right at the front are the two nostrils.
94257.m: The trunk is the elephant's nose.

94258.q: What is the space behind the nostrils called?
94258.e: Air flows through the nostrils into the nasal cavity. From there it goes on into the throat.
94258.m: Behind the nostrils is the nasal cavity.

94259.q: Why is a dog's nose usually damp around the nostrils?
a: So that it can see better
Because it always has a cold
So that it barks more quietly
94259.e: Scent particles stick well to the damp skin around the nostrils. That way the dog can notice smells even better.
94259.m: A damp dog's nose helps with smelling.

94260.q: Which bird has its nostrils right at the tip of its beak?
94260.e: The kiwi from New Zealand has its nostrils at the tip of its long beak. That way it smells worms in the ground.
94260.m: The kiwi smells with the tip of its beak.

94261.q: Which animal can close its nostrils when diving?
94261.e: Hippos spend a lot of time in water. When they go under, they close their nostrils so no water runs in.
94261.m: Hippos close their nostrils when they dive.

a: On top of the tip of the snout
94262.e: A crocodile's nostrils are on top of its snout. That way it can breathe while lying almost completely under water.
94262.m: Crocodiles breathe through nostrils on top of the snout.

94263.q: How many basic tastes are known today?
94263.e: The five basic tastes are sweet, sour, salty, bitter and umami. Everything else is a mixture or comes from smelling.

94264.q: Is it true that each part of the tongue only tastes one flavour?
a: No, all parts taste all the basic tastes
Yes, only sweet at the front and only bitter at the back
Yes, only the middle tastes anything
Yes, only the edges taste anything
94264.e: The old tongue map is wrong. All the basic tastes can be detected all over the tongue.
94264.m: The whole tongue tastes all the basic tastes.

94265.q: Is “spicy”, like chilli, a basic taste?
a: No, it is a feeling of pain and heat
Yes, it is the sixth basic taste
Yes, it is a kind of sweet
Yes, it is a kind of salty
94265.e: The substance in chilli irritates nerves that report heat and pain. That is why spicy food feels like burning.
94265.m: Spicy is a feeling of pain, not a taste.

94266.q: What does food need so that the tongue can taste it?
94266.e: Saliva dissolves the taste substances from the food. Only then can the taste buds recognise them.

94267.q: Which animal tastes with its feet?
94267.e: Butterflies have sensory cells on their feet. When they land on a flower, they can taste straight away whether there is food there.

94268.q: Which fish has taste cells over almost all of its skin?
94268.e: Catfish have taste cells all over their body. That way they find their food in murky water.
94268.m: The catfish tastes with almost all of its skin.

94269.q: Why does very cold ice cream taste less sweet than melted ice cream?
a: Cold makes the tongue less sensitive
94269.e: When it is very cold, the tongue senses sweetness less strongly. That is why melted ice cream often tastes much sweeter.

94270.e: Cats lack the sensory cell for sweet. They mainly eat meat and do not need sugar.

94271.e: Sugar tastes sweet. It is found in fruit, honey and sweets.

94272.q: Which taste do even babies especially like?
94272.e: Even babies like sweet things, and breast milk tastes slightly sweet too.
94272.m: Even babies like the sweet taste.

94273.q: What does a sweet taste tell the body?
94273.e: Sweet food contains sugar, and sugar provides energy. That is why our body likes sweet things.
94273.m: Sweet shows that there is energy in the food.

94274.q: Why should you brush your teeth after eating sweets?
a: So that your tongue gets sweeter
94274.e: Bacteria in the mouth turn sugar into acid. This acid can make holes in the teeth, called tooth decay.
94274.m: Brushing your teeth after sweet things protects against tooth decay.

94275.q: Which fruit tastes especially sweet when ripe?
94275.e: Ripe bananas contain a lot of sugar, so they taste sweet.

94276.q: How does the taste of a fruit change when it ripens?
94276.e: As it ripens, the fruit makes more sugar. Unripe fruit often tastes sour or tart.
94276.m: Ripe fruit tastes sweeter than unripe fruit.

94277.q: Which sweet syrup is made from the sap of a tree?
94277.e: Maple syrup is made from the sap of the sugar maple. The sap is boiled until a sweet syrup is left.
94277.m: Maple syrup comes from the sap of the maple tree.

94278.q: From which tall grass plant is sugar made in warm countries?
94278.e: Sugar cane is a tall grass with sweet juice. A lot of sugar is made from it in warm countries.
94278.m: Sugar cane is a sweet grass.

94279.q: Which liquid from the kitchen tastes sour?
94279.e: Vinegar contains acetic acid, which is why it tastes sour. It is used in salad dressing, for example.

94280.e: Sour food contains acid, such as citric acid or acetic acid. The tongue recognises this acid.

94281.q: What does milk that has gone off taste like?
94281.e: When milk gets old, bacteria turn the milk sugar into acid. That is why it tastes sour.
94281.m: Milk that has gone off tastes sour.

94282.q: Which dairy product tastes slightly sour?
94282.e: Yoghurt is made with bacteria that produce lactic acid. That is why yoghurt tastes slightly sour.
94282.m: Yoghurt tastes slightly sour because of lactic acid.

94283.q: Which vegetable is used for sauerkraut?
94283.e: Sauerkraut is made from finely cut white cabbage. As it ferments, lactic acid forms and makes it sour.
94283.m: Sauerkraut is made from white cabbage.

94284.q: What can a sour taste warn you about?
94284.e: Unripe fruit and spoiled food often taste sour. That way you notice that something is not good.
94284.m: Sour can warn of something unripe or spoiled.

94285.q: What face do many people pull when they bite into a lemon?
a: They screw up their eyes and mouth
94285.e: The strong sour taste makes many people pull a face. Their eyes and mouth get screwed up.
94285.m: Many people pull a face at sour things.

94286.q: Which green citrus fruit tastes very sour?
94286.e: The lime is related to the lemon. Its juice contains a lot of acid and tastes very sour.

94287.q: What do crisps usually taste like?
94287.e: Crisps are seasoned with salt. That is why they taste salty.

94288.q: Which seasoning do you sprinkle on a breakfast egg to make it taste salty?
94288.e: Table salt tastes salty. Many people sprinkle a pinch of it on a boiled egg.

94290.q: Why does our body need a little salt?
a: So that nerves and muscles work well
94290.e: Salt contains sodium, which nerves and muscles need. But too much salt is unhealthy.
94290.m: The body needs a little salt, but not too much.

94291.q: What tastes salty when it runs down your face?
94291.e: Tears contain a little salt. That is why they taste slightly salty.

94292.q: Why is salt spread on the roads in winter?
a: So that the road gets clean
So that the road gets warm
94292.e: Salt makes ice and snow melt. That way roads and pavements are less slippery.
94292.m: Road salt makes ice on the road melt.

94293.q: What does eating a lot of salty food often give you?
94293.e: Salt holds on to water in the body. That is why the body signals thirst after salty food.

94294.q: What does coffee without sugar taste like?
94294.e: Coffee contains bitter substances such as caffeine. Without sugar it therefore tastes bitter.

94295.q: What does a bitter taste often warn us about?
94295.e: Many poisonous plants taste bitter. That is why people often prefer to spit out bitter things.

94296.q: Which chocolate tastes the most bitter?
94296.e: Dark chocolate has a lot of cocoa and little sugar. Cocoa tastes bitter.
94296.m: Dark chocolate tastes more bitter than milk chocolate.

94297.q: Which vegetable often tastes a little bitter?
94297.e: Chicory contains bitter substances. That is why many children like it less.

94298.q: Why do children often like bitter things less than adults?
a: Children cannot taste bitterness at all
Bitter things are only poisonous for children
94298.e: Children react more strongly to bitterness than adults. As they get older, many get used to bitter food.

94299.q: What does the white pith under orange peel taste like?
94299.e: The white pith of an orange contains bitter substances. That is why people often pick it off.
94299.m: The white pith of an orange tastes bitter.

94300.q: Which drink made from leaves can turn bitter if it brews too long?
94300.e: If black tea brews for too long, a lot of tannins dissolve. Then it tastes bitter.
94300.m: Tea that brews too long turns bitter.

94301.q: Apart from sour, what does a grapefruit taste like?
94301.e: Grapefruits contain bitter substances. So they taste bitter and also a bit sour.

94302.q: Which red salad leaf tastes slightly bitter?
94302.e: Radicchio has red leaves with white veins. It contains bitter substances, so it tastes slightly bitter.

94303.q: Which basic taste has a name that roughly means “delicious”?
94303.e: Umami roughly means delicious. It describes a strong, savoury taste.

94304.q: Which country does the word “umami” come from?
94304.e: The Japanese scientist Kikunae Ikeda described the taste umami in 1908. He found it in a seaweed soup.
94304.m: The word umami comes from Japan.

94305.e: Stock tastes strong and savoury. This taste is called umami.

94306.q: Which cheese has a strong umami taste?
94306.e: Cheese that has matured for a long time, like Parmesan, tastes very savoury. It has a lot of umami.
94306.m: Mature cheese like Parmesan tastes umami.

94307.q: What is the substance that gives many foods their umami taste called?
94307.e: Glutamate is found naturally in many foods. The tongue has sensory cells that recognise it as umami.

94308.q: Which sauce from Asia tastes strongly umami?
94308.e: Soy sauce is made from soya beans and matured for a long time. It tastes salty and very umami.

94309.q: Which vegetable tastes especially umami when ripe and dried?
94309.e: Ripe and dried tomatoes contain a lot of the substance that tastes umami. That is why they flavour sauces so well.

94310.q: Which savoury spread from Switzerland tastes strongly umami?
94310.e: Cenovis is a savoury paste made from brewer's yeast that you spread on bread and butter. Yeast extract tastes strongly umami.
94310.m: Cenovis is a savoury Swiss yeast spread.

94311.q: Where are most of the taste buds?
94311.e: Most taste buds are on the tongue. Only a few are in other places in the mouth.
94311.m: Most taste buds are on the tongue.

94312.q: What are the little bumps on the tongue that contain taste buds called?
94312.e: The rough tongue is covered in little bumps called papillae. Many of them contain taste buds.
94312.m: Taste buds sit in the papillae of the tongue.

94313.q: Roughly how many taste buds does a person have?
94313.e: A person has several thousand taste buds. Each one is made up of many sensory cells.
94313.m: A person has a few thousand taste buds.

94314.q: What happens to the sensory cells in the taste buds after a while?
a: They are replaced by new ones
94314.e: The sensory cells only live a short time, about one to two weeks. Then new ones grow.
94314.m: Taste cells are renewed again and again.

94315.q: What often happens when you burn your tongue on hot tea?
a: You taste less for a while
You cannot smell anything any more
94315.e: Heat can injure the sensory cells on the tongue. Until new ones have grown, you taste less.
94315.m: A burnt tongue tastes less for a while.

94316.q: What does the surface of the tongue feel like?
94316.e: The many papillae make the tongue rough. The taste buds are in them too.
94316.m: The tongue is rough because of the papillae.

94317.q: What connects the taste buds to the brain?
94317.e: The sensory cells send their message along nerves to the brain. There the feeling of sweet or bitter is created.
94317.m: Nerves carry taste to the brain.

94318.q: Apart from the tongue, where else are there some taste buds?
a: On the roof of the mouth and in the throat
94318.e: Some taste buds are on the roof of the mouth and in the throat. But most are on the tongue.
94318.m: There are taste buds on the roof of the mouth too.

94319.e: A scent is a smell that we find pleasant. One example is the smell of flowers.
94319.m: A scent is a pleasant smell.

94320.q: Which purple plant smells strongly and is often put into scented bags?
94320.e: Lavender has purple flowers and a strong scent. Dried, it is put in little bags in the wardrobe.

94321.q: Why do many flowers have a scent?
94321.e: The scent attracts bees and other insects. As they visit, they carry pollen from flower to flower.

94322.q: What can you often smell in the morning at the baker's?
94322.e: Baking produces lots of scents. That is why the baker's smells of fresh bread.

94323.q: What is a scented liquid you spray on your skin called?
94323.e: Perfume contains scents from flowers, woods or the laboratory. You spray it on to smell nice.

94324.q: Where do scent particles have to go for us to smell them?
94324.e: Scent particles float in the air. We breathe them in, and the smell cells in the nose recognise them.
94324.m: Scent particles travel through the air into the nose.

94325.q: What can scents easily bring back?
94325.e: In the brain, smells quickly reach the areas for feelings and memories. That is why a scent often reminds you of the past.

94326.q: Which flower is famous for its scent and often has thorns on its stem?
94326.e: Many roses smell strongly and have thorns on the stem. Rose oil is also made from their petals.
94326.m: Roses are known for their scent.

94327.q: Why do you smell less outside in winter than in summer?
a: The nose is smaller in winter
There is no air in winter
The smell cells sleep in winter
94327.e: When it is warm, scents evaporate faster and drift through the air. In the cold there are fewer scent particles.
94327.m: Warmth spreads scents better than cold.

94328.e: A stink is a smell that we find disgusting. It often warns us about something bad.
94328.m: A stink is an unpleasant smell.

94329.q: Which animal sprays a smelly liquid when in danger?
94329.e: The skunk lives in America. When in danger, it sprays a very foul-smelling liquid at its enemies.
94329.m: The skunk defends itself with a stink.

94330.q: What does the stink of spoiled food warn us about?
a: That it is about to rain
94330.e: Spoiled food smells bad because bacteria are growing in it. Anyone who eats it can get ill.
94330.m: You should not eat food that stinks.

94331.q: What does natural gas smell of, so that a leak is noticed straight away?
a: A smelly substance that is added
94331.e: Natural gas itself hardly smells. That is why a strong-smelling substance is added, so that you smell a leak straight away.
94331.m: Natural gas is given a smell so that leaks are noticed.

94332.q: What do rotten eggs smell of?
94332.e: Rotten eggs give off a gas that contains sulphur. It smells very unpleasant.

94333.q: Which insect gives off a foul smell when disturbed?
94333.e: Stink bugs release a foul-smelling liquid when in danger. That way they scare off enemies.
94333.m: Stink bugs protect themselves with a stink.

94334.q: What should you do if your home smells of gas?
a: Open the windows and go outside
94334.e: Gas can burn or explode. That is why you let in air, leave the home and call for help outside.
94334.m: If you smell gas, let in air and go outside.

94335.q: Which giant flower stinks of rotting meat?
94335.e: The titan arum has one of the largest flower heads in the world. Its stink attracts flies and beetles that pollinate it.
94335.m: The titan arum attracts insects with its stink.

94336.q: What flows through a cable so that a lamp lights up?
94336.e: Electric current flows through the wire in the cable. It makes lamps light up and motors turn.

94337.q: Can you see the electricity in a cable?
94337.e: Electricity flows inside the wire and is invisible. You can only tell it is there from what it does, for example from the light of a lamp.
94337.m: Electricity in a cable is invisible.

94338.q: Which fish can give strong electric shocks itself?
94338.e: The electric eel lives in South America. With special organs it produces electric shocks to stun prey and fight off enemies.
94338.m: The electric eel can produce electricity.

94339.q: Which sea fish senses the weak electric signals of its prey?
94339.e: Sharks have special sense organs on their snout. With them they sense the weak electric signals of animals, even when they are hidden in the sand.
94339.m: Sharks sense the electric signals of their prey.

94340.q: Where do most trains in Switzerland get their energy from?
a: From the line above the track
94340.e: Almost the whole Swiss railway network is electrified. The trains take electricity from the overhead line above the tracks.
94340.m: Swiss trains mostly run on electricity from the overhead line.

94341.q: What is the arm on the roof of a locomotive that takes electricity from the line called?
94341.e: The pantograph presses against the overhead line from below. That way electricity flows into the locomotive and drives the motors.
94341.m: The pantograph collects electricity for the locomotive.

94342.q: What happens in a flat during a power cut?
a: The lights and appliances go off
94342.e: Without electricity, lamps, the fridge and other appliances can't work. That is why it suddenly goes dark during a power cut.
94342.m: Without electricity, lamps and appliances go off.

94343.q: Why does it sometimes crackle when you take off a woolly jumper?
94343.e: Rubbing gives the fabric an electric charge. The charge jumps across in tiny sparks, and you hear that as crackling.
94343.m: Rubbing can make tiny electric sparks.

94344.q: Who built the first battery around the year 1800?
94344.e: The Italian Alessandro Volta stacked metal discs with soaked pieces of card. This voltaic pile was the first battery.
94344.m: Alessandro Volta built the first battery.

94345.q: How many volts does an ordinary small round AA battery have?
94345.e: An ordinary AA battery gives a voltage of 1.5 volts. That is harmless to your hands.

94346.q: Which battery has two snap connectors next to each other on top?
94346.e: The 9-volt battery is a small rectangular block. On top it has two connectors that snap into place.
94346.m: The 9-volt battery has two connectors on top.

94347.q: What is a small, flat, round battery like the ones in watches called?
94347.e: Button cells are small and flat like a button. They are found in watches, scales and small toys.
94347.m: Small flat batteries are called button cells.

94348.q: Why are button cells dangerous for small children?
a: If swallowed they can cause serious injury
94348.e: A swallowed button cell can get stuck in the food pipe and injure it. That is why button cells must be kept out of reach of small children.
94348.m: Keep button cells away from small children.

94349.q: Where does a battery get its electricity from?
a: From the air in the room
94349.e: Inside the battery, chemical substances react with each other. This produces electric current until the substances are used up.
94349.m: A battery makes electricity from substances inside it.

94350.q: Why must you never throw batteries into a fire?
94350.e: In the heat, batteries can burst or explode. Poisonous substances are released.
94350.m: Batteries never go in a fire.

94351.q: What can leak out of an old battery in a device?
94351.e: Old batteries can start to leak. The liquid that comes out is corrosive and can damage the device.
94351.m: Old batteries can leak corrosive liquid.

94352.q: What happens to the lamp if a wire in the circuit comes loose?
94352.e: If a wire comes loose, the path for the electricity is broken. Then no more current can flow to the lamp.
94352.m: A loose wire breaks the circuit.

94353.q: What is a circuit that is broken somewhere called?
94353.e: If the circuit is broken at one point, it is called open. No current flows in an open circuit.
94353.m: No current flows in an open circuit.

94354.q: Why is an electric circuit called a “circuit”?
a: The current flows all the way round from terminal to terminal
The wires are always bent round
The lamp is always perfectly round
The battery turns in a circle
94354.e: The current flows from one terminal of the battery through the wires and the lamp back to the other terminal. So its path is a closed loop.
94354.m: In a circuit, the current flows all the way round back to the battery.

94355.q: What is a device in a circuit that uses electricity, like a lamp or a motor, called?
94355.e: Lamps, motors or bells need electricity to work. That is why they are called loads or consumers.

94356.q: What does a small electric motor do in a closed circuit?
94356.e: An electric motor turns electricity into a turning movement. You can use it, for example, to drive a small propeller.
94356.m: An electric motor turns when current flows.

94357.q: What do you draw in a circuit diagram instead of real pictures of the parts?
94357.e: In a circuit diagram, each component has a simple symbol. That way you can draw a circuit quickly.
94357.m: A circuit diagram shows components as simple symbols.

94358.q: How does a lamp shine with an almost flat battery?
94358.e: An almost flat battery only supplies a little energy. That is why the lamp shines more faintly.
94358.m: With an almost flat battery, the lamp shines faintly.

94359.q: What does an electric bell do when the circuit is closed?
94359.e: When current flows through the bell, a small hammer strikes a bell. That makes the ringing sound.
94359.m: A bell rings when current flows.

94360.q: What is a cable called that you use to connect a device to a socket further away?
94360.e: An extension cable has a plug at one end and a socket at the other. That way the electricity reaches further.
94360.m: An extension cable takes electricity further away.

94361.q: Why shouldn't you lay a cable under a carpet?
a: It can be damaged and get hot
94361.e: Under the carpet the cable gets stepped on and can break. Also, the heat can't escape, which is dangerous.

94362.q: What do you do with a cable reel before you plug in a powerful device?
a: You put it in the sun
You tie it in a knot
94362.e: In a cable reel that is still wound up, the cable can get very hot. That is why you unroll it completely.
94362.m: Unroll a cable reel completely before using it.

94363.q: What are the thick lines that run across the country high up on big pylons called?
94363.e: High-voltage power lines carry electricity from the power stations over long distances. They hang high up on pylons.
94363.m: High-voltage lines carry electricity over long distances.

94364.q: Where are many power cables in towns and cities?
94364.e: In towns, power cables are usually laid in the ground. There they are protected and don't get in the way.
94364.m: In towns, power cables are often in the ground.

94365.q: Why do the wires in a power cable have different coloured coverings?
a: So that you can tell them apart
So that they shine more nicely
So that animals don't eat them
94365.e: Each colour shows what a wire is for. That way the electrician can connect the wires correctly.
94365.m: The colours of the wires help to connect them correctly.

94366.q: What colour is the covering of the protective earth wire?
94366.e: The protective earth wire is striped yellow and green. If there is a fault, it carries the current away safely.
94366.m: The earth wire in a cable is yellow-green.

94367.q: Why is the inside of a power cable often made of many thin wires?
a: So that it is more colourful
94367.e: Many thin wires together are easy to bend. A single thick wire would be stiff and could break.
94367.m: Many thin wires make a cable flexible.

94368.q: What is the cable you use to charge a mobile phone called?
94368.e: Through the charging cable, electricity flows from the socket into the phone's battery. You usually also need a charger plug.
94368.m: You charge a mobile phone with a charging cable.

94369.q: What is a switch called that only lets current flow while you press it, as with a doorbell?
94369.e: A push button only closes the circuit while you press it. When you let go, the circuit is open again.
94369.m: A push button only works while you press it.

94370.q: What is a switch that lets you make the light brighter or dimmer called?
94370.e: With a dimmer you can adjust the brightness of a lamp smoothly. The word comes from “dim”.
94370.m: With a dimmer you adjust the brightness.

94371.q: Why does the light on the staircase often go off by itself after a while?
a: A timer switch turns it off
94371.e: Many staircases have a timer switch. It turns the light off after a few minutes and so saves electricity.
94371.m: A timer switch turns the light off by itself.

94372.q: What switches on an outdoor light when someone walks past?
94372.e: A motion sensor notices when someone moves. Then it switches the light on for a short time.
94372.m: A motion sensor switches on the light when something moves.

94373.q: What is the red switch you use to stop a machine immediately in an emergency called?
94373.e: The emergency stop button is usually red on a yellow background. Pressing it stops the machine immediately.
94373.m: The emergency stop button stops a machine immediately.

94374.q: What does the symbol “0” on a switch mean?
94374.e: On many devices, “I” stands for on and “0” for off. When the switch is at “0”, no current flows.
94374.m: The zero on a switch means off.

94375.q: Two switches are one after the other in the same circuit. One is open. What does the lamp do?
94375.e: When the switches are connected one after the other, the current has to flow through both. If one is open, the path is broken.
94375.m: Connected in series, all switches must be closed.

94376.q: What is the small switch in the middle of the cable of a floor lamp called?
94376.e: On many floor and table lamps, the switch is right in the cable. It is called an inline switch.
94376.m: An inline switch sits in the lamp's cable.

94377.q: What lights up in an incandescent light bulb?
94377.e: In an incandescent bulb, current flows through a thin wire. The wire gets so hot that it glows brightly.
94377.m: In a light bulb, a thin wire glows.

94378.q: Which metal is the filament of a light bulb made of?
94378.e: Tungsten only melts at a very high temperature. That is why it can stand the strong glowing.
94378.m: The filament is made of tungsten.

94379.q: Which inventor made the light bulb practical for everyday use around 1880?
94379.e: The American Thomas Edison improved the light bulb so that it lasted a long time. After that it was used in many homes.
94379.m: Thomas Edison made the light bulb well known.

94380.q: Why shouldn't you touch a light bulb that has just been on?
94380.e: A light bulb gets very hot when it is shining. You can burn your fingers on it.
94380.m: A light bulb that is on is hot.

94381.q: What do you say when a light bulb stops working because its wire has broken?
94381.e: Over time the filament gets thinner and breaks. Then people say the bulb has blown.
94381.m: If the filament breaks, the bulb has blown.

94382.q: What is the part of a light fitting that you screw the bulb into called?
94382.e: The socket holds the bulb firmly and connects it to the electricity. You screw the bulb in by its thread.
94382.m: The light bulb is screwed into the socket.

94383.q: What is the round outer part of a light bulb made of?
94383.e: The outer part of a light bulb is a glass bulb. The light shines out through the glass.
94383.m: The outer part of a light bulb is made of glass.

94384.q: Why doesn't the filament burn up straight away inside the glass bulb?
a: There is no oxygen in the bulb
The wire is made of wood
94384.e: Burning needs oxygen. Inside the glass bulb there is no air, or only a gas without oxygen.
94384.m: Without oxygen, the filament doesn't burn up.

94385.q: What do you do first before changing a light bulb?
94385.e: When changing a bulb, you touch parts that may carry electricity. That is why you switch off the electricity first.
94385.m: Switch off the electricity before changing a bulb.

94386.q: What does the abbreviation LED stand for?
94386.e: LED is short for “light-emitting diode”. It is a tiny electronic part that gives off light.

94387.q: How long does an LED lamp last compared with an incandescent bulb?
94387.e: LED lamps last for many years, much longer than incandescent bulbs. That is why you rarely need to change them.
94387.m: LED lamps last much longer than incandescent bulbs.

94388.q: Does an LED get as hot as an incandescent bulb when it shines?
a: Yes, it gets just as hot
94388.e: An LED turns electricity mainly into light and only a little heat. That is why it gets much less hot.
94388.m: An LED stays fairly cool when it shines.

94389.q: What happens if you connect an LED to a battery the wrong way round?
94389.e: A diode only lets current through in one direction. The wrong way round, no current flows and it stays dark.
94389.m: An LED only lights up the right way round.

94390.q: Which leg of an LED is connected to the positive terminal?
94390.e: A simple LED has two little legs. The longer one goes to the positive terminal, the shorter one to the negative terminal.
94390.m: The long leg of the LED goes to plus.

94391.q: What does a small glowing LED light on a device often show?
94391.e: Many devices have a small indicator light. When it is on, the device is switched on or charging.
94391.m: A small light often shows that a device is on.

94392.q: How big is a single LED usually?
94392.e: LEDs are often only a few millimetres in size. That is why lots of them fit into a lamp or a screen.

94393.q: What are the pixels of many big scoreboards in stadiums made of?
94393.e: Big scoreboards are made of thousands of small LEDs. Together their dots of light make pictures and numbers.
94393.m: Big scoreboards are made of lots of LEDs.

94394.q: Which sign marks the positive terminal of a battery?
94394.e: The positive terminal has the plus sign. That way you know which way round the battery goes.
94394.m: The positive terminal has a plus sign.

94395.q: Which end of a round AA battery is the positive terminal?
a: The end with the small bump
94395.e: On round batteries, the positive terminal has a small bump. The flat end is the negative terminal.
94395.m: The bump on the battery is the positive terminal.

94396.q: How many terminals does a battery have?
94396.e: Every battery has a positive and a negative terminal. Current only flows when both are connected through a circuit.

94397.q: What do the signs + and − in the battery compartment of a device show?
a: How to put the battery in
94397.e: Plus and minus are marked in the battery compartment. The terminals of the battery must match them exactly.
94397.m: The signs in the battery compartment show the right direction.

94398.q: What often happens if a battery in a torch is the wrong way round?
94398.e: If the batteries are the wrong way round, plus and minus don't match up. Then no current flows through the lamp.
94398.m: Batteries put in the wrong way round leave the lamp dark.

94399.q: What colour is the cable for the positive terminal often, for example in a car?
94399.e: In a car, the cable for the positive terminal is usually red. The cable for the negative terminal is often black.
94399.m: Plus is often red and minus often black.

94400.q: How many volts does an ordinary car battery have?
94400.e: Most cars have a 12-volt battery. It supplies, for example, the electricity to start the engine.
94400.m: A car battery usually has 12 volts.

94401.q: What happens if you connect the positive and negative terminals of a battery directly with a wire?
a: The wire and battery get hot
94401.e: This is called a short circuit. A lot of current flows, and the wire and battery get hot. That is why you should never do it.
94401.m: A short circuit makes the wire and battery hot.

94402.q: Does a dry wooden spoon conduct electricity?
a: Yes, just as well as metal
Yes, but only a thick spoon
94402.e: Dry wood hardly lets electricity through. That is why wood is called an insulator.

94403.q: Does a metal spoon conduct electricity?
94403.e: Metals let electricity through well. So a metal spoon is a conductor.

94404.q: Which of these objects is an insulator?
94404.e: A rubber (eraser) is made of rubber or plastic. These materials don't conduct electricity; the other things are made of metal.

94405.q: Which of these objects conducts electricity?
94405.e: A paper clip is made of metal and conducts electricity. Rubber, wood and glass are insulators.
94405.m: A metal paper clip conducts electricity.

94406.q: Is glass a conductor or an insulator?
94406.e: Glass doesn't let electricity through. That is why glass is an insulator.

94407.q: Does the human body conduct electricity?
a: Yes, that is why electricity is dangerous
94407.e: The body contains a lot of water with salts, so it conducts electricity. That is why an electric shock can be dangerous.

94408.q: Does dry air normally conduct electricity?
94408.e: Dry air is normally an insulator. Only at a very high voltage, such as with lightning, can electricity jump through the air.

94409.q: Why do power lines hang from parts made of glass or porcelain?
a: So that no electricity flows into the pylon
So that the line looks nicer
So that birds can nest there
94409.e: Glass and porcelain are insulators. They hold the line in place without electricity flowing into the pylon.
94409.m: Porcelain parts keep electricity away from the pylon.

94410.q: Which materials conduct electricity especially well?
94410.e: All metals conduct electricity, and some do so especially well. That is why wires are made of metal.

94411.q: What colour is a freshly polished piece of copper?
94411.e: Copper is a metal with a reddish-brown colour. That makes it easy to recognise.

94412.q: What colour does a copper roof turn after many years outdoors?
94412.e: Copper slowly reacts with air and rain. A green layer forms that protects the metal.
94412.m: Copper roofs turn green over time.

94413.q: Which famous statue in New York is made of copper on the outside and is therefore green?
94413.e: The Statue of Liberty is covered with thin copper sheets. Over time they turned green.
94413.m: The Statue of Liberty is made of copper and so it is green.

94414.q: What is the chemical symbol for copper?
94414.e: The symbol Cu comes from the Latin word “cuprum”. That is the Latin name for copper.
94414.m: The symbol for copper is Cu.

94415.q: Which metal conducts electricity even better than copper but is much more expensive?
94415.e: Silver conducts electricity best of all. Because it is expensive, copper is usually used for cables.
94415.m: Silver conducts even better than copper.

94416.q: What is the golden-yellow mixture of copper and zinc that trumpets are often made of called?
94416.e: Brass is mainly made of copper and zinc. It shines golden yellow and is used for wind instruments and door handles.
94416.m: Brass is a mixture of copper and zinc.

94417.q: Which mixture of copper and tin has been used for bells for a long time?
94417.e: Bronze is made of copper and tin. Bronze bells sound beautiful and last a very long time.
94417.m: Bronze is a mixture of copper and tin.

94418.q: Why do some saucepans have a copper base?
94418.e: Copper conducts not only electricity but also heat very well. That is why the pan heats up quickly and evenly.

94419.q: What is copper obtained from in mines?
94419.e: Copper is found in certain rocks called copper ores. In mines it is dug out of them and purified.

94420.q: Why must you never climb an electricity pylon?
a: There is a danger of death from electricity
Because it is too cold up there
94420.e: Power lines with a very high voltage hang from pylons. Even near them, you can get a deadly electric shock.

94421.q: How many volts does the overhead line above the SBB railway tracks carry?
94421.e: The SBB overhead line carries 15,000 volts. That is much more than in a socket and deadly dangerous.
94421.m: The SBB overhead line has 15,000 volts.

94422.q: Why must you never climb onto a railway carriage?
a: Electricity from the overhead line can jump across
The carriage has just been painted
94422.e: Electricity from the overhead line can jump through the air to a person. So you don't have to touch anything at all to get hurt.
94422.m: Climbing onto railway carriages is deadly dangerous.

94423.q: What do you do first if someone is still touching a device with electricity?
94423.e: Anyone who touches the person will get an electric shock too. So first pull out the plug or switch off the fuse, and get help.
94423.m: In an electrical accident, first switch off the electricity.

94424.q: Which emergency number do you call in Switzerland for an ambulance?
94424.e: The number 144 calls the ambulance service. 117 is the police and 118 the fire brigade. On 147, children and young people can talk about their worries.
94424.m: In Switzerland, you reach an ambulance on 144.

94425.q: What must you never put into a socket?
94425.e: Metal conducts electricity. Anyone who puts scissors or a nail into a socket gets a dangerous electric shock.
94425.m: Only a plug belongs in a socket.

94426.q: What does a yellow warning sign with a black lightning arrow mean?
94426.e: The yellow triangle with the lightning arrow warns of electrical voltage. You find it on electricity boxes and pylons.
94426.m: The lightning sign warns of electricity.

94427.q: Why doesn't a bird sitting on a power line get an electric shock?
94427.e: The bird sits on only one wire and touches nothing else. So no current flows through its body.
94427.m: A bird on just one wire stays safe.

94429.q: Why do you unplug a charger from the socket after charging?
a: It saves electricity and is safer
So that it charges faster next time
So that the cable doesn't rust
So that the socket stays clean
94429.e: A charger that is plugged in uses a little electricity even without a phone. Unplugging it saves energy and lowers the risk of fire.

94430.q: What do you need if a plug from another country doesn't fit into a Swiss socket?
94430.e: Many countries have different sockets. A travel adapter safely connects the foreign plug to the Swiss socket.
94430.m: For foreign plugs you need an adapter.

94431.q: Who should repair a broken socket in the flat?
94431.e: Working on electric wiring is dangerous and needs expert knowledge. That is why a trained professional does it.

94432.q: What do you do if a socket gives off sparks or looks broken?
a: Don't use it and tell an adult
94432.e: A broken socket can cause an electric shock or a fire. You don't use it and tell an adult straight away.

94433.q: What does a socket in the garden often have so that no rain gets in?
94433.e: Outdoor sockets have a lid that closes by itself. That way the inside stays dry.
94433.m: Outdoor sockets have a protective lid.

94434.q: How can you often tell that a plug in the socket has become too hot?
94434.e: If a plug gets too hot, plastic melts and there is a burning smell. Then an adult should switch off the electricity.
94434.m: A burning smell at a socket is a warning sign.

94435.q: Why does a multi-socket extension often have its own switch?
a: To switch off all devices at once
94435.e: With the switch on the extension, you disconnect all the devices plugged into it at the same time. That saves electricity used on standby.
94435.m: With the switch on the extension you switch everything off.

94536.q: Which structural unit forms the basic framework of all silicate minerals?
94536.e: In all silicates, a silicon atom is surrounded tetrahedrally by four oxygen atoms. How these tetrahedra are linked determines the silicate class.
94536.m: Every silicate is built from silicon-oxygen tetrahedra.

94537.q: Roughly what share of the Earth's crust do silicate minerals make up?
94537.e: Oxygen and silicon are the most common elements in the Earth's crust. Accordingly, well over 90 per cent of crustal rocks consist of silicates.
94537.m: The Earth's crust consists almost entirely of silicates.

94538.q: Which usually green silicate mineral is a main component of the upper mantle?
94538.e: Olivine is rich in magnesium and iron and makes up a large part of the upper mantle. Green olivine grains are often found in basalt lava.
94538.m: Olivine is the most important mineral of the upper mantle.

94539.q: Which common silicate mineral is so hard that it scratches glass?
94539.e: Quartz has a hardness of 7 on the Mohs scale and is harder than window glass. Talc, on the other hand, is the softest mineral on the scale.
94539.m: Quartz is hard enough to scratch glass.

94540.q: Which silicate mineral can be split into thin, flexible sheets?
94540.e: Mica is a sheet silicate whose layers are only weakly held together. That is why it can be split into wafer-thin sheets that often glitter.
94540.m: Mica splits into thin, shiny sheets.

94541.q: Which well-known gemstones are varieties of the mineral beryl?
94541.e: Emerald is green beryl, aquamarine blue beryl. Ruby and sapphire, by contrast, are varieties of the mineral corundum.

94542.q: Which sheet silicate is the main component of china clay?
94542.e: Kaolinite, Al₂Si₂O₅(OH)₄, forms when feldspars weather. As kaolin it is the most important raw material for porcelain.
94542.m: Porcelain is made from the clay mineral kaolinite.

94543.q: What does the term “mafic” mean for silicate minerals?
94543.e: The word is formed from magnesium and the Latin ferrum for iron. Mafic minerals such as olivine or pyroxene are usually dark, felsic ones such as quartz and feldspar light.
94543.m: Mafic minerals are dark and rich in magnesium and iron.

94544.q: Which three minerals is granite mainly made of?
94544.e: Granite is a plutonic rock made of light quartz, mostly light or reddish feldspar and dark mica. A well-known German mnemonic goes: “Feldspat, Quarz und Glimmer, die drei vergess ich nimmer” (feldspar, quartz and mica, those three I'll never forget).
94544.m: Granite consists of feldspar, quartz and mica.

94545.q: Which mineral crystallises first from a basalt melt in the discontinuous series?
94545.e: Olivine forms at the highest temperatures. As the temperature falls, pyroxene follows, then other silicates with more strongly linked tetrahedra.
94545.m: Olivine crystallises first from a basalt melt.

94546.q: Which mineral crystallises at the end of Bowen's reaction series at the lowest temperatures?
94546.e: The last remaining melt is rich in SiO₂, potassium and water. From it, potassium feldspar, muscovite and finally pure silicon dioxide crystallise.
94546.m: Quartz is the last mineral in Bowen's series.

94547.q: What does Bowen's reaction series describe?
a: The order in which minerals crystallise from cooling magma
The order of the layers in a glacier
The sequence of weathering at the surface
94547.e: In the early 20th century, Norman Bowen showed that minerals crystallise from the melt in a fixed order depending on temperature. Olivine forms first, quartz last.
94547.m: Bowen's series orders minerals by their crystallisation temperature.

94548.q: Why is quartz much more resistant to weathering at the Earth's surface than olivine?
a: It crystallises at a lower temperature, closer to conditions at the surface
It is radioactive and therefore stable
It contains a lot of iron
94548.e: Minerals that crystallise at high temperatures are not very stable at the cool surface and weather faster. That is why sand is mostly quartz, while olivine breaks down quickly.
94548.m: What crystallises last from magma weathers most slowly.

94549.q: Which rock forms when an SiO₂-rich residual melt solidifies slowly deep underground?
94549.e: At the end of Bowen's series, a melt rich in SiO₂, potassium and sodium remains. If it solidifies slowly deep down, large crystals of quartz, feldspar and mica grow, in other words granite. Gabbro is low in SiO₂ and pumice solidifies at the surface.
94549.m: Granite forms from SiO₂-rich melt deep underground.

94550.q: In the discontinuous branch, what happens to early-formed crystals if they stay in contact with the remaining melt?
a: They react to form a new mineral
94550.e: As the temperature falls, the early-formed crystals are no longer stable and react with the melt. This produces a mineral with a different crystal structure, hence the name reaction series.
94550.m: In Bowen's series, crystals react with the melt to form new minerals.

94551.q: What is the process called in which early-formed crystals are separated from the melt so that the remaining melt becomes richer in SiO₂?
94551.e: If heavy, early-formed crystals sink, they can no longer react with the melt. The melt therefore changes its composition step by step.
94551.m: Fractional crystallisation lets different rocks form from one magma.

94552.q: At roughly what temperature does a basalt melt begin to crystallise?
94552.e: Basaltic melts begin to crystallise at about 1200 °C. Granitic residual melts, on the other hand, only solidify at about 650 to 700 °C.
94552.m: Basalt magma starts to solidify at about 1200 °C.

94553.q: What is meant by metamorphism in geology?
a: The transformation of rock by pressure and temperature without melting
The wearing away of rock by wind and water
The solidifying of a melt at the Earth's surface
The deposition of sediments in the sea
94553.e: In metamorphism, new minerals and textures form in the solid state. If the rock melts, it is no longer called metamorphism.
94553.m: Metamorphism changes rock in the solid state.

94554.q: Which rock forms from limestone through metamorphism?
94554.e: Under pressure and heat, the calcite of limestone recrystallises into a granular texture. Fossils and layering are usually lost in the process.

94555.q: What happens to a metamorphic rock if the temperature gets so high that it melts completely?
a: Magma forms, which later becomes an igneous rock
94555.e: Metamorphism takes place in the solid state. If the rock melts, the igneous part of the rock cycle begins, for example with the formation of granite.

94556.q: Which rock forms from mudstone in high-grade regional metamorphism, after it has passed through phyllite and mica schist?
94556.e: As the grade of metamorphism rises, mudstone turns in turn into slate, phyllite, mica schist and finally gneiss. The minerals get larger and larger.
94556.m: Gneiss is a high-grade metamorphic rock.

94557.q: What is the difference between contact and regional metamorphism?
a: Contact: heat from a body of magma, regional: pressure and heat during mountain building
Contact: only under water, regional: only on land
Contact: from meteorites, regional: from wind
94557.e: In contact metamorphism, the surrounding rock around a magma chamber is heated. Regional metamorphism affects large areas that are buried deep during mountain building.
94557.m: Contact metamorphism is local, regional metamorphism is large-scale.

94558.q: What does a rock that can only form at very high pressure tell you if you find it at the surface today?
a: It was once very deep in the Earth, for example in a subduction zone
It was made artificially by humans
94558.e: High-pressure rocks such as eclogite form at depths of dozens of kilometres. During mountain building they were lifted up again, as near Zermatt.
94558.m: High-pressure rocks show that rock had sunk deep down.

94559.q: What causes the foliation in regional metamorphic rocks?
a: Minerals lining up at right angles to the main pressure
94559.e: Flaky minerals such as mica prefer to grow at right angles to the direction of greatest pressure. The rock can then be split along these surfaces.
94559.m: Foliation is caused by directed pressure.

94560.q: What are minerals called that have the same chemical formula but different crystal structures?
a: Polymorphs, for example diamond and graphite
Alloys, for example bronze and brass
Mixtures, for example granite and gneiss
94560.e: Diamond and graphite both consist of pure carbon. Which form develops depends on pressure and temperature; diamond needs very high pressure.
94560.m: Same formula, different structure: this is called polymorphism.

94561.q: Why does pressure in sinking rock rise faster than temperature in subduction zones?
a: The cold ocean plate sinks quickly and warms up only slowly
The sun only heats the surface
There is no geothermal heat in subduction zones
94561.e: Rock conducts heat poorly, so the sinking plate stays cool for a long time. Typical rocks are then ones such as blueschist, which indicate high pressure at low temperature.
94561.m: In subduction zones, rock stays cool for a long time despite great depth.

a: The melt cools slowly deep underground
They are worn smooth by rivers
They cool quickly in the air
94562.e: Deep down, the surrounding rock is hot and insulates the melt. The crystals have plenty of time to grow and become visible to the naked eye.
94562.m: Slow cooling deep down produces large crystals.

94563.q: Which three main minerals make up granite?
94563.e: Granite is a light, SiO₂-rich plutonic rock. A well-known German mnemonic goes: “Feldspat, Quarz und Glimmer, die vergess ich nimmer” (feldspar, quartz and mica, I'll never forget them).
94563.m: Granite consists of feldspar, quartz and mica.

94564.q: What distinguishes a plutonic rock such as granite from a volcanic rock such as basalt?
a: It solidifies deep in the Earth's crust instead of at the surface
94564.e: Plutonic rocks cool slowly deep down and become coarse-grained. Volcanic rocks solidify quickly at the surface and are fine-grained or glassy.
94564.m: Plutonic rocks solidify deep down, volcanic rocks at the surface.

94565.q: Where does the plutonic rock get its name from?
a: From Pluto, god of the underworld, because it forms deep down
From the dwarf planet Pluto, where it comes from
From the Greek word for gold
94565.e: Plutonic rocks form when magma solidifies deep in the Earth's crust. The name recalls Pluto, the Roman god of the underworld.
94565.m: Plutonic rocks are named after Pluto, god of the underworld.

94566.q: By what does the QAPF diagram of the Swiss geologist Albert Streckeisen classify plutonic rocks?
a: By the proportions of their main minerals
By the country where they were found
94566.e: The diagram uses the proportions of quartz, alkali feldspar, plagioclase and feldspathoids. It is used worldwide to name plutonic rocks.
94566.m: The Streckeisen diagram classifies plutonic rocks by their mineral content.

94567.q: What is an extremely coarse-grained dyke rock called that forms from water-rich residual melts?
94567.e: Water and other volatile substances make the residual melt runny and help crystals grow. This produces crystals from centimetres to metres in size, often with rare elements.
94567.m: Pegmatites contain giant crystals from the last residual melt.

94568.q: What is a very large plutonic body with an exposed area of over 100 square kilometres called?
94568.e: Batholiths usually consist of many individual intrusions and reach deep into the crust. One example is the Sierra Nevada Batholith in California.
94568.m: A batholith is a giant plutonic body.

94569.q: Which ultramafic plutonic rock consists mainly of olivine and makes up the upper mantle?
94569.e: Peridotite contains more than 40 per cent olivine as well as pyroxenes. It is the most common rock in the upper mantle.
94569.m: The upper mantle consists mainly of peridotite.

94570.q: Why are volcanic rocks fine-grained or glassy?
a: The lava cools quickly at the surface
94570.e: With rapid cooling, the crystals have hardly any time to grow. With very rapid cooling, glass with no crystal lattice even forms.
94570.m: Rapid cooling produces fine-grained volcanic rocks.

94571.q: What is the black, glassy volcanic rock with a shell-like fracture called?
94571.e: Obsidian forms when SiO₂-rich lava solidifies so quickly that no crystals grow. In the Stone Age, sharp blades were made from it.

94572.q: Why can pumice float on water?
a: It is full of gas bubbles
It contains a lot of fat
94572.e: In an explosive eruption, gas-rich lava foams up and solidifies immediately. The many holes make the rock lighter than water.

a: Large crystals in a fine-grained groundmass
94573.e: Some crystals already grow slowly in the magma chamber, while the rest solidifies quickly during the eruption. This produces a two-stage texture.
94573.m: A porphyritic texture reveals two cooling stages.

94574.q: Which volcanic rock corresponds chemically to granite?
94574.e: Rhyolite is SiO₂-rich and light like granite, but fine-grained because it cooled quickly. It often forms in explosive eruptions.
94574.m: Rhyolite is the volcanic counterpart of granite.

94575.q: Which volcanic rock is the most widespread on Earth?
94575.e: Basalt forms the ocean floor and therefore most of the Earth's surface. It forms at mid-ocean ridges and at hotspots such as Hawaii or Iceland.
94575.m: The seabed consists mainly of basalt.

94576.q: How do the hexagonal columns of columnar basalt form?
a: Through shrinkage of the lava as it cools
94576.e: As it cools, the lava contracts and cracks at regular intervals. The cracks usually form five- or six-sided columns at right angles to the cooling surface.
94576.m: Columnar basalt forms through shrinkage cracks.

94577.q: Why is SiO₂-rich lava thicker than lava low in SiO₂?
a: The silicate tetrahedra are more strongly linked
94577.e: With more SiO₂, the tetrahedra link into chains and networks even in the melt. Such lava is also usually cooler, which makes it even thicker.
94577.m: The more SiO₂ a lava contains, the more slowly it flows.

a: A piece of oceanic lithosphere on land
A salt dome under the desert
94578.e: Ophiolites are sequences of rock from the mantle and oceanic crust that were pushed onto continents at plate boundaries. They give an insight into the structure of the ocean floor.
94578.m: In an ophiolite you can study the seabed on land.

94579.q: Which rock forms the uppermost igneous layer of a complete ophiolite sequence?
94579.e: From bottom to top come mantle rock, gabbro, a dyke swarm and pillow lavas, with deep-sea sediments on top. Pillow lavas form when basalt flows out under water.
94579.m: Pillow lavas show that lava solidified under water.

94580.q: Where does the oceanic crust that is found in ophiolites on land form?
a: At mid-ocean ridges, where plates drift apart
94580.e: At the ridges, magma rises and solidifies into new crust while the plates drift apart. Ophiolites are pieces of this crust that were later pushed onto continents.
94580.m: Ocean crust forms at mid-ocean ridges.

94581.q: What is the pushing of oceanic lithosphere onto the edge of a continent called?
94581.e: In subduction an oceanic plate sinks, whereas in obduction it is pushed over the edge of the continent. Only in this way are parts of the ocean floor preserved on land.
94581.m: Obduction is the opposite of subduction.

94582.q: In which country is the Semail Ophiolite, one of the largest and best-exposed ophiolites in the world?
94582.e: The Semail Ophiolite covers about 100,000 square kilometres. It formed in the Late Cretaceous and was then pushed onto the edge of the Arabian plate.
94582.m: In Oman, a huge piece of former ocean floor lies at the surface.

94583.q: On which Mediterranean island are the Troodos Mountains, a famous piece of former ocean floor?
94583.e: The Troodos Mountains consist of an almost complete ophiolite sequence. In the 1960s they helped scientists understand how ocean crust forms at spreading zones.
94583.m: The Troodos Mountains on Cyprus are former ocean floor.

94584.q: Where in Switzerland are well-known ophiolites from the former Piedmont-Liguria Ocean found?
94584.e: Around Zermatt and Saas Fee, serpentinites, metagabbros and pillow lavas of an ancient ocean are exposed. They were buried deep during the formation of the Alps and lifted out again.
94584.m: Near Zermatt, remains of an ancient ocean floor lie in the Alps.

94585.q: Into which rock is the mantle rock of an ophiolite often converted by taking up water?
94585.e: Olivine and pyroxene react with seawater to form serpentine minerals. The greenish, often shiny rock is also widespread in the Alps.
94585.m: Water turns mantle rock into serpentinite.

a: The hardening of loose sediment into sedimentary rock
94586.e: Under increasing weight from above and at moderate temperatures, loose sediments become solid rock. Diagenesis covers all changes after deposition up to metamorphism.
94586.m: Diagenesis turns loose sediment into solid rock.

94587.q: What is the process called in which sediment is squeezed by the weight above and loses pore water?
94587.e: As the covering grows, the grains move closer together. Clays in particular lose a large part of their original pore space.

94588.q: What is the cementing of sediment grains by minerals precipitated in the pores called?
94588.e: Minerals such as calcite, quartz or iron oxides precipitate from the pore water. They glue the grains together into solid rock.
94588.m: A cement of minerals holds sedimentary rocks together.

94589.q: Which sedimentary rock forms through diagenesis from angular rock debris?
94589.e: Angular fragments show that the material was hardly transported. Once hardened it is called breccia, whereas rounded pebbles give a conglomerate.
94589.m: A breccia consists of cemented angular fragments.

94590.q: What is the transformation of peat via lignite into hard coal called?
94590.e: With increasing burial, pressure and temperature, the carbon content rises while water and volatile substances escape. Anthracite is at the end of the series.
94590.m: In coalification, plant material becomes coal.

94591.q: What is the transformation of limestone into dolomite rock by magnesium-rich solutions called?
94591.e: Magnesium from the pore water replaces some of the calcium in calcite. This forms the mineral dolomite, CaMg(CO₃)₂, which makes up large parts of the Dolomites.
94591.m: Dolomite forms when magnesium is built into limestone.

94592.q: At roughly what temperature does diagenesis turn into metamorphism?
94592.e: The boundary is gradual and lies at about 150 to 200 °C. Above this, typical metamorphic minerals form.

94593.q: What happens during pressure solution in limestone?
a: Lime is dissolved at points of high pressure and carried away
Lime melts because of the pressure
Lime takes up water and swells
94593.e: At grain contacts under high pressure, calcite dissolves and is deposited again elsewhere. What remains are jagged, dark seams of insoluble clay, called stylolites.
94593.m: Pressure solution leaves jagged seams in limestone.

94594.q: Why does a layer that settled out of muddy water often have coarse grains at the bottom and fine ones at the top?
a: Coarse grains sink faster than fine ones
Fine grains are heavier than coarse ones
The fine grains are brought later by the wind
94594.e: Heavy, coarse grains sink first, while fine ones stay suspended for longer. So the grain size in the layer decreases upwards; this is called graded bedding.
94594.m: Coarse grains settle faster than fine ones.

94595.q: What does the Hjulström diagram show?
a: At which current speeds grains are eroded, transported or deposited
How minerals crystallise as they cool
94595.e: The diagram compares flow speed and grain size. It shows, for example, that sand is eroded most easily, while fine clay needs more current because of its cohesion.
94595.m: The Hjulström diagram links current and grain size.

94596.q: How do you order gravel, sand and clay by grain size, from coarse to fine?
94596.e: Gravel has the largest grains and sand is in the middle. Clay is so fine that you can no longer see the individual grains.
94596.m: From coarse to fine: gravel, sand, clay.

94597.q: What can be read from cross-bedding in a sandstone?
a: The former direction of the current
94597.e: Cross-beds form on the downstream side of moving ripples or dunes. They slope in the direction of the current.
94597.m: Cross-bedding shows where the wind or water came from.

94598.q: What do symmetrical ripple marks indicate?
a: A wave motion swinging back and forth
A current in one direction only
94598.e: Waves move the water at the bottom back and forth, which creates symmetrical ripples. Current ripples, by contrast, are asymmetrical.
94598.m: Symmetrical ripples are made by waves.

94599.q: What is true of the age of undisturbed sediment layers?
a: The lower layers are older than the upper ones
The upper layers are older than the lower ones
All layers are the same age
The thickest layers are always the oldest
94599.e: Sediments are deposited one after another, with the new material always on top. This law of superposition applies as long as the layers have not been folded or thrust over.
94599.m: In undisturbed layers, the older ones are at the bottom.

94600.q: What does the rounding of pebbles tell you about how they were transported?
a: Well-rounded pebbles were usually transported a long way
Angular pebbles were transported a long way
The rounding depends only on the colour
94600.e: When transported in a river, the stones knock against each other and lose their edges. The longer the journey, the rounder they usually become.
94600.m: The further a pebble travels, the rounder it becomes.

94601.q: What does the Molasse of the Swiss Plateau mainly consist of?
94601.e: During the formation of the Alps, debris was dumped into the foreland basin to the north. This produced sandstones, marls and conglomerate (Nagelfluh), which shape the Swiss Plateau today.
94601.m: The Molasse is the debris of the young Alps.

94602.q: Up to roughly what age can radiocarbon dating be used?
94602.e: After about nine half-lives, so little C-14 is left that it can hardly be measured. Older samples need isotopes with a longer half-life.
94602.m: The C-14 method only works for the last few tens of thousands of years.

94603.q: In uranium-lead dating, which isotope decays with a half-life of about 4.5 billion years?
94603.e: Uranium-238 decays via many intermediate stages to lead-206, with a half-life of about 4.47 billion years. Uranium-235 decays much faster to lead-207.
94603.m: Uranium-238 has about the same half-life as the age of the Earth.

94604.q: A sample still contains an eighth of the original amount of a radioactive isotope. How many half-lives have passed?
94604.e: After each half-life, the amount halves: 1/2, 1/4, 1/8. So an eighth is reached after three half-lives, because 2³ = 8.
94604.m: Each halving corresponds to one half-life.

94605.q: Which mineral is particularly suitable for uranium-lead dating?
94605.e: As it grows, zircon takes in uranium but hardly any lead. It is also very tough, so the clock is preserved for billions of years.
94605.m: Zircons are the most accurate clocks in geology.

94606.q: How old are the oldest dated mineral grains on Earth, from the Jack Hills in Western Australia?
94606.e: Individual grains from the Jack Hills gave an age of about 4.4 billion years. They show that there was solid crust shortly after the Earth formed.
94606.m: The oldest minerals on Earth are over four billion years old.

94607.q: Why is the potassium-argon method well suited to volcanic rocks?
a: The noble gas argon escapes from the melt
94607.e: In liquid lava, the gaseous argon escapes, so the clock is then set to zero. Only after solidifying does new argon-40 build up from the decay of potassium-40.
94607.m: An eruption resets the potassium-argon clock to zero.

94608.q: Why is the ratio of parent to daughter isotope measured in radiometric dating?
a: Because decay happens at a steady rate and so works like a clock
Because the ratio changes with the weather
Because daughter isotopes make the rock harder
Because this determines the colour of the rock
94608.e: Radioactive isotopes decay with a fixed half-life. The more daughter isotope has built up compared with the parent isotope, the older the rock.
94608.m: Radioactive decay is a natural clock in rock.

94609.q: In 1956 Clair Patterson determined the age of the Earth to be about 4.55 billion years. What did he study to do this?
a: Growth rings of very old trees
94609.e: Meteorites formed at the same time as the Earth and have stayed unchanged since. Patterson used lead from the Canyon Diablo meteorite, and his value is still almost unchanged today.
94609.m: The age of the Earth was determined using lead from meteorites.

94610.q: What is a rock thin section?
a: A wafer-thin ground slice of rock for the microscope
A fine crack in a rock
A rock ground smooth by a glacier
A thin sheet of pressed sand
94610.e: A slice of rock is glued onto glass and ground down to a few hundredths of a millimetre. Then light shines through it and the minerals can be identified under the microscope.
94610.m: A thin section makes rock see-through under the microscope.

94611.q: Which instrument is used to study a rock thin section?
94611.e: The polarising microscope works with polarised light. Many minerals show typical colours in it and can be told apart this way.
94611.m: Thin sections are studied under a polarising microscope.

94612.q: Why do many minerals in a thin section show bright colours between crossed polarising filters?
a: They refract light by different amounts depending on direction
They glow by themselves like glow-worms
94612.e: Many crystals are birefringent: light travels through them at different speeds depending on direction. Between crossed filters this produces colours that are typical of the mineral.
94612.m: Birefringence makes minerals look coloured under the microscope.

94613.q: What can you see under the microscope in a thin section of granite?
a: The individual mineral grains such as quartz, feldspar and mica
The temperature of the Earth's core
94613.e: Granite consists of quartz, feldspar and mica. In a thin section you can see the shape, size and arrangement of these grains and draw conclusions about how the rock formed.
94613.m: A thin section shows which minerals a rock is made of.

94614.q: Why are rocks ground so thin for microscopy?
a: So that most minerals become see-through
94614.e: At normal thickness, most rocks are opaque. Only in thin slices do most minerals let light through and show their optical properties.
94614.m: Rocks only become see-through in thin slices.

94615.q: How are ore minerals studied that stay black and opaque in a thin section?
a: In reflected light on polished sections
With a UV lamp in the dark
94615.e: Opaque minerals do not let light through, but they reflect it differently. Under a reflected light microscope they can be recognised by their reflection colour and reflectivity.
94615.m: Ore minerals are identified in reflected light.

94616.q: How do you determine in a thin section what percentage of a rock consists of a particular mineral?
a: You count which mineral lies at many evenly spaced points
You weigh the whole thin section
You measure the thickness of the section
You judge the colour of the rock with the naked eye
94616.e: The section is moved in even steps and the mineral under the crosshairs is noted each time. Hundreds of points give the share of each mineral.
94616.m: Point counting measures the mineral content of a rock.

94617.q: What does archaeology use thin sections of pottery fragments for?
a: To find out where the clay used came from
To work out the weight of the vessels
To change the colour of the glaze
94617.e: Mineral and rock grains embedded in the clay reveal the area the raw material came from. This makes it possible to reconstruct trade routes.
94617.m: Thin sections show where the clay of ancient pottery came from.

94618.q: With crossed polarisers, how are the polariser and the analyser positioned relative to each other?
94618.e: The analyser then only lets through light whose direction of vibration has been changed in the mineral. Without a sample the image stays black.
94618.m: With crossed polarisers the empty field of view is dark.

94619.q: What do geologists use a polarising microscope for?
a: To identify minerals in wafer-thin slices of rock
To measure the age of fossils
To observe stars in the night sky
94619.e: Minerals change polarised light in typical ways. This makes it possible to recognise the components of a rock.
94619.m: A polarising microscope is used to identify minerals in rock.

94620.q: Which property of anisotropic minerals causes the interference colours in a polarising microscope?
94620.e: In the crystal, light is split into two rays travelling at different speeds. After the analyser, the path difference leads to interference and therefore to colours.
94620.m: Birefringence produces the bright colours in a polarising microscope.

94621.q: Why is rock ground into a very thin slice (thin section) for the polarising microscope?
a: So that light shines through the minerals
So that the rock becomes lighter
So that the rock is no longer radioactive
So that it fits on a postage stamp
94621.e: A thin section is only about 0.03 millimetres thick. This makes most minerals transparent so they can be examined in transmitted light.
94621.m: A thin section is so thin that light shines through it.

a: Light that vibrates in only one direction
Light that comes from the North Pole
94622.e: Ordinary light vibrates in all directions at right angles to its direction of travel. A polarising filter lets through only one direction of vibration.
94622.m: Polarised light vibrates in only one direction.

94623.q: A mineral such as biotite changes colour in polarised light when it is rotated. Why is that?
a: It absorbs light to different degrees depending on the direction of vibration
It reflects the colour of the lamp
94623.e: Coloured crystals absorb light to different degrees depending on direction. This is called pleochroism; biotite, for example, changes between light and dark brown.
94623.m: Some minerals change colour in polarised light.

94624.q: Through which clear mineral do you see writing double because it refracts light doubly to a very strong degree?
94624.e: Clear calcite, also called Iceland spar, splits a ray of light into two rays. That is why everything you look at through it appears double.
94624.m: Calcite refracts light so strongly in two that you see images double.

94625.q: To which mineral group, the most common in the Earth's crust, does plagioclase belong?
